r-tlayudas.summary: A large crisp tortilla with beans, quesillo, grilled tasajo, lettuce and avocado.
r-tlayudas.history: A specialty of the central valleys of Oaxaca, often sold in markets and at evening street stalls.
steps: Heat a comal over medium heat. Spread a thin layer of asiento, if using, and beans on each tlayuda.
Add quesillo and heat until the base is crisp and the cheese melts, without burning the tortilla.
Grill the tasajo separately until its center reaches 63 °C; rest 3 minutes and cut into strips.
Add meat, lettuce and avocado. Spoon on salsa, fold and serve immediately.
tips: Use a thin layer of beans to keep the tortilla crisp.
sources: Cocina tradicional oaxaqueña, notas de mercado 20 de Noviembre

r-mole-negro.summary: A home version of the Oaxacan sauce made with dried chiles, seeds, nuts and chocolate, with a dark color and silky texture.
r-mole-negro.history: Mole negro is part of festive cooking in Oaxaca. Ingredients and techniques vary between families and communities; this version uses a shorter ingredient list for home cooking.
ingredients: 3 black chilhuacle chiles, 2 mulato chiles and 2 pasilla chiles, stems and seeds removed
30 g almonds and 30 g unsalted peanuts
1/2 teaspoon cinnamon, 2 cloves and 4 black peppercorns
1 liter chicken stock, plus extra if needed
steps: Toast the chiles briefly on each side without burning. Soak in hot water 20 minutes, then drain.
Heat the lard in a casserole. Brown the sesame seeds, nuts and plantain separately, removing each before it burns.
Blend the chiles, tomatoes, onion, garlic, bread, spices and browned ingredients in batches with some stock to make a fine paste.
Fry the paste over medium-low heat for 10 minutes, stirring constantly. Add the remaining stock and chocolate.
Simmer gently for 60-90 minutes, stirring frequently. Add stock if too thick and adjust the salt. The sauce should coat a spoon.
tips: Add chocolate gradually and taste: some tablets contain a lot of sugar.
sources: Recetario familiar de los Valles Centrales

r-chiles-nogada.summary: Poblano peppers filled with meat and fruit, covered with walnut sauce and pomegranate.
r-chiles-nogada.history: Associated with Puebla and September celebrations, the dish combines seasonal fruit with a creamy walnut sauce.
ingredients: 400 g mixed ground beef and pork
30 g raisins and 30 g chopped almonds
Seeds of 1 pomegranate and 2 tablespoons chopped parsley
steps: Roast the peppers until blistered. Cover 10 minutes, peel carefully and slit one side to remove the seeds.
Sauté onion and garlic in oil. Add and break up the meat, then add tomatoes, fruit, raisins, almonds and cinnamon.
Cook the filling 20-25 minutes until the liquid reduces and the meat reaches 71 °C. Season.
Blend walnuts, cheese and milk into a creamy sauce, adding milk gradually to control its thickness.
Fill the peppers, cover with walnut sauce and decorate with pomegranate and parsley. Serve immediately; refrigerate the sauce if made ahead.
tips: Drain the filling before stuffing the peppers so it does not dilute the walnut sauce.

r-birria.summary: Beef simmered in a dried-chile marinade and served with broth and tortillas.
r-birria.history: Associated with Jalisco, birria has many regional and family versions, including beef preparations served in tacos.
ingredients: 1.5 kg stewing beef, cut into chunks
1 teaspoon ground cumin and 1 teaspoon dried oregano
1 onion, half for cooking and half chopped for serving
steps: Toast the chiles lightly and soak 15 minutes. Blend with garlic, cumin, oregano, vinegar and 250 ml of the water; strain.
Coat the meat and marinate covered in the refrigerator for 1 hour.
Place in a pot with bay leaves, half the onion and the remaining water or stock. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer gently for about 3 hours until easily shredded.
Shred the meat and adjust the broth seasoning. Serve in hot tortillas with onion, cilantro and broth on the side.
tips: The meat is ready when it pulls apart with a fork; if still firm, continue simmering gently.

r-gumbo.summary: Louisiana stew with chicken, andouille and vegetables, thickened with a dark flour-and-oil roux.
r-gumbo.history: Gumbo is a signature Louisiana dish shaped by African, French and Creole culinary traditions.
ingredients: 500 g boneless chicken, cut into pieces
1 onion, 2 celery stalks and 1 green bell pepper, chopped
steps: Heat the oil in a heavy pot and add flour. Stir over medium-low heat for 20-30 minutes until chocolate brown; start again if it burns.
Carefully add onion, celery and pepper. Cook 8 minutes; add garlic and sausage and stir 2 minutes.
Gradually stir in the stock. Add chicken, bay leaf, thyme and Cajun seasoning.
Simmer for 40-50 minutes until the chicken is tender and reaches 74 °C. Remove the bay leaf and adjust the salt.
Serve the gumbo in bowls with the cooked rice.
tips: Keep stirring the roux and stay by the pot: it can quickly go from toasted to burnt.
sources: Cocina cajún y criolla de Luisiana

r-brisket.summary: Slow-smoked beef brisket with a pepper-and-salt crust.
r-brisket.history: Brisket is central to Texas barbecue, where long cooking over gentle heat develops its tender texture.
steps: Prepare the smoker at 110-120 °C with cooking-safe wood. Trim excess fat, leaving a thin layer.
Coat the beef with salt and pepper. Smoke over indirect heat until a crust forms and the center approaches 70 °C.
Wrap in smoking paper and continue to about 93 °C, until a probe slides in with little resistance. Thickness affects timing; allow about 10 hours for cooking.
Rest wrapped for 1 hour under hot-holding conditions, then slice against the grain just before serving.
tips: Temperature is a guide; probe resistance and resting determine the slicing texture.
sources: Tradición del BBQ de Texas Hill Country

r-pizza.summary: Fermented dough topped with tomato, mozzarella and basil, adapted for a home oven.
r-pizza.history: Neapolitan pizza is known for fermented dough, an airy rim and intense heat. This home adaptation uses prepared dough and provides domestic oven instructions.
ingredients: 150 g drained fior di latte mozzarella
steps: Preheat the oven with a pizza stone or heavy baking tray at its maximum temperature, around 250-275 °C, for 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into two balls. Stretch by hand on a lightly floured surface, keeping the rim thicker.
Add tomato, salt and well-drained mozzarella. Bake each pizza 8-12 minutes until the rim browns and the base is cooked.
Add basil and oil after baking. In a dedicated pizza oven at 450 °C, cooking may take just 60-90 seconds.
tips: Drain the mozzarella thoroughly to avoid a wet center.

r-cacio.summary: Roman pasta with an emulsion of pecorino and black pepper.
r-cacio.history: A Roman classic built around pasta, pecorino cheese and black pepper.
steps: Cook the pasta in lightly salted water according to its package. Reserve 300 ml of cooking water before draining.
Toast the pepper in a dry pan for 30 seconds. Add 2 tablespoons of the pasta water.
Mix the cheese with a little lukewarm pasta water in a bowl to make a cream; very hot water can make it clump.
Add pasta to the pan, turn off the heat and stir in the cheese cream. Add water by the spoonful until glossy. Serve immediately.
tips: Add cheese off the heat and use lukewarm water to prevent clumps.

r-okonomiyaki.summary: Savory cabbage pancake topped with sauce, mayonnaise and bonito flakes.
r-okonomiyaki.history: An Osaka street-food specialty whose name refers to cooking what you like on a griddle.
ingredients: 5 g bonito flakes and 1 teaspoon aonori
steps: Mix flour, eggs and water. Fold in the cabbage without compressing it.
Heat oil in a skillet over medium heat. Form two thick pancakes and lay the pork belly on top.
Cook 5 minutes, turn with a wide spatula and cover. Cook 5-7 minutes more until the center is firm and the pork is cooked.
Turn again and check that no liquid batter remains. Top with sauce, mayonnaise, bonito flakes and aonori.
tips: Do not press the pancake with the spatula: steam helps cook the cabbage inside.

r-ramen.summary: Shoyu-style ramen with chicken stock and dashi, cooked pork and marinated egg. A quick version using prepared broth and toppings.
r-ramen.history: Tokyo-style shoyu ramen helped popularize ramen in the postwar period.
steps: Heat the chicken stock and dashi. Mix soy sauce and mirin and add gradually, checking the salt.
Heat the chashu separately until hot throughout. Keep the eggs refrigerated until serving.
Cook the noodles in a separate pot according to the package; drain without leaving them to stand.
Divide broth and noodles between two bowls. Add chashu, halved eggs and scallions. Serve immediately.
tips: Cook the noodles last and serve immediately so they do not absorb too much broth.

r-padthai.summary: A vegetarian adaptation of Thai stir-fried noodles with tofu, egg, tamarind and peanuts.
r-padthai.history: Pad Thai combines rice noodles with sweet, sour and savory seasonings; this home version uses tofu and soy sauce.
steps: Soak the noodles according to the package and drain. Mix tamarind, sugar, soy sauce and 3 tablespoons water.
Heat the oil and brown the tofu. Push aside, add the eggs and scramble until set.
Add noodles and sauce. Stir-fry 2-4 minutes, adding water by the spoonful if needed, until tender.
Add sprouts and scallions and cook until the sprouts are hot. Serve with peanuts and lime.
tips: Measure and prepare everything before heating the wok because cooking is quick.

r-khaosoi.summary: Northern Thai coconut curry noodle soup with chicken, crisp noodles and pickles.
r-khaosoi.history: Associated with Chiang Mai and northern Thailand, khao soi combines a rich curry broth with soft and crisp noodles.
ingredients: 300 g boneless chicken thigh, cut into pieces
2 tablespoons prepared khao soi curry paste
steps: Heat 1 tablespoon oil and fry the curry paste 1 minute. Add coconut milk and stock.
Add chicken and simmer gently 20-25 minutes until tender and at 74 °C.
Cook the noodles according to the package. Drain and reserve a small portion; fry it in the remaining oil until crisp.
Serve the curry over cooked noodles and top with crisp noodles, pickles, onion and lime.
tips: Taste the curry paste before adding salt; concentration varies between brands.

r-tacos-pastor.summary: Thin slices of marinated pork served in corn tortillas with pineapple, onion and cilantro.
r-tacos-pastor.history: Tacos al pastor are closely associated with Mexico City and the Mexican adaptation of vertical-spit cooking. This skillet version preserves the marinade and pineapple for home cooking.
ingredients: 1/2 chopped onion and 3 tablespoons chopped cilantro
1 tablespoon oil and salt to taste
steps: Soak the chiles in hot water for 15 minutes. Blend with achiote, garlic, orange juice, vinegar, cumin, oregano and salt.
Coat the pork and marinate covered in the refrigerator for 2 hours.
Heat the oil and cook the meat in batches without crowding, until browned and at 63 °C; rest 3 minutes.
Brown the pineapple separately, chop the meat and serve in hot tortillas with pineapple, onion and cilantro.
tips: Cook pork in small batches to brown it without liquid pooling in the pan.

r-tiramisu.summary: Layers of coffee-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone cream, finished with cocoa.
r-tiramisu.history: Tiramisu is associated with Treviso and northeastern Italy. Different claims exist about its creation.
steps: Beat the pasteurized yolks with sugar until thick. Fold in mascarpone without overbeating.
In a clean bowl, beat the pasteurized whites to stiff peaks and fold gently into the cream.
Briefly dip ladyfingers in cold coffee. Layer them in a dish and cover with cream; repeat.
Cover and refrigerate at least 4 hours. Dust with cocoa just before serving and keep refrigerated.
tips: Use cold coffee and dip the biscuits briefly so the layers keep their shape.

r-pancakes.summary: Soft breakfast pancakes made with buttermilk and served with maple syrup.
r-pancakes.history: Buttermilk pancakes are common throughout the United States and are not assigned here to a particular state.
ingredients: 30 g melted butter, plus extra for the pan
steps: Mix flour, baking powder, sugar and salt. Separately beat buttermilk, egg and cooled melted butter.
Fold together just until no dry flour remains, leaving some lumps.
Grease a skillet over medium heat. Add small portions and cook until bubbles appear and the edges look matte, about 2 minutes.
Turn once and cook 1-2 minutes more until cooked through. Serve with maple syrup.
tips: Leave some lumps in the batter; overmixing makes pancakes tough.

r-mochi.summary: Soft rice-flour sweets enclosing strawberries and red bean paste.
r-mochi.history: Daifuku is a Japanese confection made with a soft mochi wrapper; strawberry is a popular filling variation.
steps: Wrap each dried strawberry in 20 g of anko and set aside.
Mix rice flour, sugar and water in a heatproof bowl. Steam 15-20 minutes, stirring halfway, until shiny and translucent.
Carefully turn onto a starch-dusted surface and let cool enough to handle; the dough is very sticky.
Divide into six pieces, flatten and wrap around each strawberry. Seal, brush off excess starch and cool before eating.
tips: Hot mochi dough is sticky and can burn: let it cool enough before handling.

r-guacamole.summary: Mashed avocado with onion, chile, cilantro, tomato and lime.
r-guacamole.history: A Mexican avocado preparation with regional and household variations. Its use is widespread and is not assigned to one city.
ingredients: Juice of 1 lime and salt to taste
steps: Halve the avocados, remove the pits and scoop out the flesh.
Mash with a fork, leaving some texture. Add onion, chile, cilantro and tomato.
Gradually add lime juice, adjust salt and mix without blending.
Serve immediately with tortilla chips. If needed, cover directly against the surface and refrigerate.
tips: Mash with a fork to retain small pieces of avocado.

r-somtam.summary: Crunchy green papaya salad with lime, fish sauce, vegetables and peanuts.
r-somtam.history: Green papaya salad is associated with Laos and northeastern Thailand and has many regional variations. This Thai version does not attribute its exclusive origin to Bangkok.
steps: Pound garlic and chile in a mortar. Mix lime juice, fish sauce and sugar.
Add beans and tomatoes and gently press to release some juice without puréeing them.
Add papaya, alternating gentle pounding with spoon movements until coated.
Adjust the balance of salt, acidity and heat. Top with peanuts and serve immediately.
tips: Gently pound the papaya so it absorbs dressing while staying crisp.

r-jambalaya.summary: Louisiana rice cooked with chicken, andouille, shrimp, vegetables and Cajun seasoning.
r-jambalaya.history: A Creole rice dish associated with Louisiana, combining meats, seafood and aromatic vegetables.
ingredients: 1 onion, 2 celery stalks and 1 green bell pepper, chopped
2 tablespoons oil and 1 teaspoon Cajun seasoning
steps: Brown chicken and sausage in oil in a wide pot. Add onion, celery, pepper and garlic; sauté 8 minutes.
Add tomatoes and Cajun seasoning and cook 5 minutes. Add rice and stock, stir once and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on low for 18 minutes. Add shrimp on top, cover and cook another 5-7 minutes until opaque and the chicken reaches 74 °C.
Turn off the heat and rest covered 5 minutes. Fluff gently and adjust the salt.
tips: Avoid constantly stirring the rice during cooking or it can turn mushy.

r-cemita.summary: A sesame bun filled with breaded beef, quesillo, avocado, chipotle and pápalo.
r-cemita.history: A classic market snack associated with Puebla.
ingredients: 2 already breaded beef cutlets, 150 g each
steps: Heat a layer of oil in a skillet and fry the cutlets on both sides until golden and the meat reaches 63 °C.
Drain and rest 3 minutes. Open the buns and spread with avocado.
Fill with cutlets, quesillo and chipotle to taste.
Add pápalo, close and serve immediately.
tips: Start with a little pápalo because its aroma is strong.

r-mxn-machaca-huevo.dishName: Machaca con huevo (shredded dried beef with eggs)
r-mxn-machaca-huevo.summary: Dried, shredded beef cooked with eggs, tomato, onion, and chile — the cornerstone of a Sonoran breakfast.
r-mxn-machaca-huevo.history: It was born from the need to preserve meat in the desert: the beef was salted, sun-dried, and pounded in a molcajete. That dried product, machaca, became a pillar of the ranch-style breakfast of the northwest, especially in Sonora, where it is served with freshly made flour tortillas.
steps: If the machaca is very dry, soak it a few minutes in warm water and drain.
Sweat the onion and chile; add the tomato and cook until it releases its juices.
Stir in the machaca and sauté so it absorbs the flavors.
Pour in the beaten eggs and stir until set but not dried out.
Serve hot with flour tortillas and salsa to taste.
tips: Taste the machaca before adding salt: dried meat may season the whole mixture.

r-mxn-caldo-queso.dishName: Caldo de queso sonorense (Sonoran cheese soup)
r-mxn-caldo-queso.summary: A light potato and green chile broth with milk and cubes of regional fresh cheese that melt as you serve it.
r-mxn-caldo-queso.history: A humble, comforting dish from the mountains and valleys of Sonora, cooked with whatever was on hand: potato, roasted green chile, and the fresh cheese from the ranches. It's everyday food that makes the most of the regional cheese and is served with a flour tortilla.
ingredients: 2 Anaheim green chiles, roasted, peeled, and cut into strips
1 tablespoon oil and salt to taste
steps: Sauté the onion and tomato until they form a base.
Add the chile strips and the potatoes; stir for a couple of minutes.
Pour in the broth and cook until the potato is tender.
Lower the heat, add the milk, and warm through without letting it boil.
Divide the cheese cubes among the bowls and ladle the soup over them so they melt.
tips: Put cheese in the serving bowl and pour hot broth over it to retain soft pieces.

r-mxn-coyotas.dishName: Coyotas de Villa de Seris (piloncillo-filled pastries)
r-mxn-coyotas.summary: Flat flour pastries filled with piloncillo and baked golden, a classic of Hermosillo.
r-mxn-coyotas.history: These cookie-empanadas originated in Villa de Seris, now part of Hermosillo, where families of bakers made them popular. Their name is linked to the region's cultural blending, and the classic piloncillo filling reflects the wheat-flour baking traditions of northern Mexico.
ingredients: 250 g piloncillo (raw cane sugar), grated or in pieces
steps: Mix the flour with the salt and lard until you get a sandy texture.
Add the water little by little and knead into a soft dough; let it rest.
Form thin disks; place piloncillo on half of them and cover with another disk, sealing the edges.
Prick the surface with a fork so the steam can escape.
Bake at 180 °C for about 20 minutes until golden.
tips: Rest the dough 20 minutes before rolling and seal well to keep the piloncillo inside.
sources: Repostería tradicional de Villa de Seris, Hermosillo

r-mxn-chilorio.summary: Shredded pork fried in a sauce of dried chiles, garlic, and spices, typical of Sinaloa.
r-mxn-chilorio.history: Chilorio began as a preservation method in Sinaloa: cooked pork was shredded and simmered in an adobo with plenty of lard, which allowed it to keep for weeks. Today it is an emblematic dish eaten in tacos and burritos made with flour tortillas.
steps: Cook the pork in salted water until tender; shred it and reserve the broth.
Soak the chiles in hot water and blend them with garlic, cumin, oregano, and vinegar.
Fry the shredded pork in lard until it begins to brown.
Strain the adobo over the meat and cook over medium heat, stirring, until it dries out and comes together.
Adjust the salt and serve in tacos or burritos.
tips: Reserve cooking stock and add a few spoonfuls if the marinade dries before combining.

r-mxn-aguachile.summary: An adaptation of Sinaloan aguachile with cooked shrimp, lime, serrano, cucumber and red onion.
r-mxn-aguachile.history: Originating on the Sinaloa coast, aguachile is a preparation of fresh shrimp 'cooked' in lime and chile. Unlike ceviche, it is served immediately to keep the seafood juicy; the green version with serrano and cilantro is the most widespread.
ingredients: 500 g fresh shrimp, peeled and butterflied
steps: For a cooked-shrimp version, boil the shrimp until firm and opaque; immediately cool in ice water and drain.
Blend lime juice, serrano, cilantro, salt and pepper into a green sauce.
Mix cold shrimp with sauce and add cucumber and red onion.
Serve immediately with tostadas and refrigerate leftovers. Lime adds acidity but does not replace cooking seafood.
tips: Add lime shortly before serving to preserve the cucumber and onion texture.

r-mxn-cabrito-pastor.summary: Milk-fed kid goat skewered on a rod and slowly roasted over charcoal, an icon of Monterrey.
r-mxn-cabrito-pastor.history: Goat came to the northeast with the goat herding introduced by Sephardic and Spanish settlers. In Nuevo León it became a celebration dish: the milk-fed kid is splayed open, skewered on a rod, and roasted vertically in front of the coals until the skin is golden and crisp.
ingredients: 1 milk-fed kid goat, cleaned and splayed open
Chile salsa and guacamole to taste
steps: Salt the goat inside and out and skewer it on the rod.
Set the rod beside the charcoal fire, skin facing outward.
Roast slowly, turning the piece so it cooks evenly, about two and a half hours.
At the end, move the skin close to the coals so it browns and crackles.
Cut into pieces and serve with flour tortillas, salsa, and guacamole.
tips: Use indirect heat and a thermometer: thick pieces must reach at least 63 °C and rest 3 minutes.

r-mxn-frijoles-charros.summary: Brothy beans with bacon, chorizo, hot dog, and chile — the classic side for northern grilled meats.
r-mxn-frijoles-charros.history: Tied to the cowboy culture of the north, frijoles charros were cooked over an open fire to feed the ranch hands. In Nuevo León they accompany the weekend carne asada; the broth carries cured meats, tomato, onion, and chile, and is served in a little clay mug.
steps: Cook the beans with onion and salt until tender.
Separately, fry the bacon and chorizo; add the sliced hot dog and brown.
Add tomato, onion, and chile and sauté into a base.
Pour this sauté into the pot of beans with their broth and boil for a few minutes.
Sprinkle with cilantro, adjust the salt, and serve hot.
tips: Dried-bean cooking time depends on their age; add hot water if the level drops before they soften.

r-mxn-discada.summary: A mix of meats and cured sausages cooked outdoors on a plow disc, a northern gathering feast.
r-mxn-discada.history: The discada makes use of an old plow disc as a concave griddle over the fire. It's a get-together dish in the north, where bacon, chorizo, beef, pork, and vegetables are added in layers. Chihuahua and its neighboring states share it as an outdoor party dish.
steps: On the hot disc, fry the bacon until it renders its fat.
Add the chorizo and then the pork; cook until browned.
Stir in the beef and sear the meat.
Add tomato, onion, and chile; pour in the beer and let it reduce.
Season and serve in flour tortilla tacos.
tips: Brown meats in batches: crowding cools the griddle and makes them simmer in their juices.

r-mxn-asado-puerco.dishName: Asado de puerco chihuahuense (Chihuahua-style pork in red chile)
r-mxn-asado-puerco.summary: Pork stewed in a red chile sauce with spices, served at parties and family meals.
r-mxn-asado-puerco.history: Also called asado rojo, it is a festive stew from Chihuahua in which pork is cooked in an adobo of the region's dried chiles. It's made for weddings, baptisms, and gatherings and served with rice and flour tortillas.
ingredients: 1 pinch each of cumin and oregano
steps: Brown the pork in lard and set aside.
Soak the chiles and blend them with garlic, cumin, and oregano; strain the sauce.
Fry the sauce in the same pot until it changes color.
Return the meat, add bay leaf and a little water, and cook over low heat until tender.
If you want more body, dissolve a tablespoon of flour in water and stir it in; adjust the salt.
tips: Mix 1 tablespoon flour with 2 tablespoons cold water before adding it to prevent lumps.

r-mxn-caldillo-durango.summary: A brothy beef stew with green chile and tomato, the signature dish of Durango.
r-mxn-caldillo-durango.history: Caldillo is the most representative dish of Durango, a legacy of ranch life in the semi-desert. In its classic version it's made with dried or fresh beef, roasted green chile, and tomato, forming a light broth eaten with a flour tortilla.
ingredients: 3 green chiles, roasted, peeled, and cut into strips
steps: Sear the beef in hot oil with the onion and garlic.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down.
Stir in the green chile strips.
Pour in the broth and simmer over low heat until the meat is tender and the stew is flavorful.
Adjust the salt and serve with flour tortillas.
tips: Start with 1 liter stock and add more for a brothier stew; the beef cut determines the final cooking time.

r-mxn-asado-boda.dishName: Asado de boda zacatecano (Zacatecas wedding stew)
r-mxn-asado-boda.summary: Pork in a sweet-and-sour sauce of dried chiles with chocolate and spices, a ceremonial stew of Zacatecas.
r-mxn-asado-boda.history: Asado de boda is the great party dish of Zacatecas, traditionally served at weddings and engagements as an offering from the groom's family. Its thick sauce combines colorado and guajillo chiles with chocolate, orange peel, and spices — the result of the sweet and smoky flavors of the north-central region.
ingredients: 3 garlic cloves, bay leaf, clove, and pepper
1 bolillo roll or fried tortilla, to thicken
steps: Brown the pork in lard and set aside.
Soak the chiles and blend them with garlic, spices, orange peel, and the fried bread.
Strain the adobo and fry it in the pot until it thickens.
Add the chocolate and let it melt into the sauce.
Return the meat, cover with water, and simmer over low heat until tender and the sauce is thick.
tips: Use a thin strip of orange peel without white pith to avoid excessive bitterness.
sources: Imagen Zacatecas: tradición del asado de bodas

r-mxn-carne-asada.dishName: Tacos de carne asada norteños (northern grilled beef tacos)
r-mxn-carne-asada.summary: Skirt or flank steak grilled over coals, chopped and served in a tortilla with guacamole, spring onions, and salsa.
r-mxn-carne-asada.history: In the north, carne asada is more than a dish — it's a weekend ritual of family togetherness. In Coahuila and the rest of the region, beef cuts are grilled over charcoal or mesquite and eaten in tacos with grilled spring onions, guacamole, and fresh salsa.
steps: Season the meat with salt, pepper, and lime juice.
Get the charcoal or mesquite coals glowing red-hot.
Grill the meat to your liking, flipping it only once.
Grill the spring onions alongside the meat.
Chop the meat and serve in tacos with guacamole, spring onions, and salsa.
tips: Check 63 °C in the thickest part and rest 3 minutes before slicing against the grain.
sources: Tradición de la carne asada norteña

r-mxn-tacos-pescado.dishName: Tacos de pescado estilo Baja (Baja-style fish tacos)
r-mxn-tacos-pescado.summary: Battered, fried fish in a corn tortilla with cabbage, crema, salsa, and lime — the hallmark of Ensenada.
r-mxn-tacos-pescado.history: Battered fish tacos are emblematic of the Baja California coast, especially Ensenada. They pair white fish battered and fried with fresh toppings like shredded cabbage, crema, and citrusy salsas — a reflection of the Pacific's abundant fishing and the ingenuity of street stalls.
ingredients: 600 g white fish fillet, cut into strips
Oil for frying and salsa to taste
steps: Make a batter by whisking the flour with the beer and salt until it's like a light pancake batter.
Dip the fish strips in the batter.
Fry them in hot oil until golden; drain.
Warm the tortillas and place the fish on them.
Top with cabbage, crema, salsa, and a few drops of lime.
tips: Keep beer cold and fry in batches at 175-180 °C; check that the fish reaches 63 °C.

r-mxn-almejas-tatemadas.summary: Chocolata clams roasted over coals and aromatic branches, a specialty of Loreto.
r-mxn-almejas-tatemadas.history: Almejas tatemadas are an ancestral dish of Loreto, Baja California Sur, where shellfish consumption dates back to pre-Hispanic times, as the region's shell middens attest. The chocolata clams are set in gravel and covered with chamizo or romerillo branches that, as they burn, give the clams their characteristic smoky flavor.
ingredients: Chamizo or romerillo branches (or aromatic firewood)
steps: Clean the clams well and set them hinge-side down on a bed of gravel or a grill.
Cover them with the chamizo or romerillo branches.
Light the branches and let the heat and smoke cook the clams for about 40 minutes.
Remove them once the shells open and the insides are cooked.
Serve with lime, salt, and hot sauce.
tips: Use live clams from a food supplier and discard broken ones or those that stay closed after cooking.

r-mxn-carne-tampiquena.dishName: Carne asada a la tampiqueña (Tampico-style grilled beef plate)
r-mxn-carne-tampiquena.summary: A grilled strip of beef fillet served with an enchilada, chile strips, beans, and guacamole — a creation of Tampico.
r-mxn-carne-tampiquena.history: The dish was conceived in the 20th century by Tampico restaurateur José Inés Loredo, who brought together on a single plate a beef fillet cut lengthwise and grilled, with representative sides: an enchilada, chile strips, beans, and guacamole. It spread across the country as a restaurant dish.
ingredients: 2 beef fillets cut into long strips
steps: Season the strip of fillet with salt and pepper.
Grill it to the desired doneness.
Prepare the enchiladas and sauté the chile strips with onion.
Warm the refried beans and make the guacamole.
Serve the meat with the enchilada, the chile strips, the beans, and the guacamole on the same plate.
tips: This recipe starts with prepared enchiladas, beans and guacamole; warm them before grilling the meat.

r-mxc-pollo-san-marcos.dishName: Pollo de San Marcos (San Marcos-style chicken)
r-mxc-pollo-san-marcos.summary: Browned chicken bathed in a dried-chile sauce with a sweet touch of fruit and wine.
r-mxc-pollo-san-marcos.history: A festive dish tied to the San Marcos National Fair in Aguascalientes; it combines chiles, spices, and fruit in a festive, comforting sauce.
steps: Cook the chicken pieces with onion, garlic, and salt until tender; reserve the broth.
Rehydrate the chiles in hot water and blend them with the tomato, garlic, onion, and spices.
Fry the strained sauce in lard until it thickens and season with a little broth.
Add the wine and the chopped fruit; bring to a boil.
Return the chicken to the sauce and cook over low heat for 20 minutes so it takes on the flavor.
Serve with red rice, pot beans, and freshly made tortillas.
tips: Keep the sauce at a gentle simmer to preserve the fruit and check 74 °C in the chicken.

r-mxc-enchiladas-mineras.summary: Tortillas dipped in guajillo sauce, filled with cheese and topped with browned potato and carrot.
r-mxc-enchiladas-mineras.history: A working-class craving from the mines of the city of Guanajuato; it was served hot and hearty to the workers and is now an emblem of the city.
ingredients: 2 garlic cloves and a piece of onion
Lettuce, onion, and cheese to serve
steps: Rehydrate the guajillos and blend them with garlic, onion, and salt; strain the sauce.
Cook the cubed potatoes and carrots and sauté them until browned.
Dip each tortilla in the sauce and fry it lightly in lard.
Fill with cheese, fold, and arrange on the plate.
Coat with more sauce and top with the potatoes and carrots.
Serve with lettuce, onion, and cheese on top.
tips: Cook potatoes and carrots until tender but firm before browning them.

r-mxc-guacamayas.summary: A crusty bolillo roll filled with pork chicharrón, pico de gallo, and a very spicy chile de árbol salsa.
r-mxc-guacamayas.history: A street snack born in the San Juan de Dios neighborhood of León around the 1950s; today there are guacamayerías with decades of tradition.
ingredients: Pico de gallo: tomato, onion, and cilantro
steps: Grind the toasted chiles de árbol with the roasted tomato, garlic, and salt into a spicy salsa.
Slit the rolls open along one side and remove some of the crumb.
Fill with the broken-up chicharrón.
Add pico de gallo and douse with the chile de árbol salsa.
Adjust with lime juice and salt and serve immediately.
tips: Fill the rolls just before serving so the pork crackling retains some texture.
sources: Aderezo OEM, comida callejera de León

r-mxc-gorditas-queretanas.summary: Thick gorditas of coarsely ground corn, filled with stews and bathed in red salsa.
r-mxc-gorditas-queretanas.history: A legacy of the Querétaro semi-desert, especially Tolimán and Bernal; in 2012 they were declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of the state.
ingredients: Filling: cheese, pressed chicharrón, or a stew
Serrano chiles and tomato for the salsa
steps: Knead the cracked corn with salt into a firm, textured dough.
Form thick gorditas and toast them on a griddle until browned on both sides.
Slit them open along one side and fill them with the stew of your choice.
Make a coarsely ground salsa of tomato and serrano.
Bathe the gorditas with the salsa and finish with chopped lettuce.
tips: Make gorditas evenly thick and cook over medium heat so the centers do not remain raw.

r-mxc-enchiladas-potosinas.summary: Tortillas made from masa kneaded with ancho chile, filled with cheese and onion, and browned on a griddle.
r-mxc-enchiladas-potosinas.history: A classic snack of San Luis Potosí in which the chile goes into the masa rather than in a separate sauce; they're sold at supper stalls and fairs.
ingredients: Crema, avocado, and cheese to serve
steps: Rehydrate the ancho chiles and blend them with garlic and salt.
Knead the chile into the masa until you get an even red color.
Form small tortillas and cook them lightly on a griddle.
Fill with cheese and onion, fold into a half-moon, and press the edge.
Fry in lard until crisp on the outside.
Serve with crema, avocado, and more cheese.
tips: Drain the chiles before blending and add the purée gradually so the dough does not get too wet.

r-mxc-zacahuil.summary: A giant tamal of coarse masa and pork in adobo, wrapped in banana leaf and baked in a wood-fired oven.
r-mxc-zacahuil.history: From the Nahuatl zacahuilli, 'big tamal'; a ceremonial dish of the Huasteca Potosina region made to share at weddings, baptisms, and village festivals.
steps: Blend the rehydrated chiles with garlic and spices to make the adobo.
Mix the coarse masa with lard and part of the adobo until smooth.
Marinate the raw pork in the rest of the adobo.
Spread the masa over the banana leaves and place the meat on top.
Wrap it up tightly into a large parcel and tie it.
Bake over low heat for several hours until the meat and masa are fully cooked.
tips: Bake the covered parcel around 160 °C for about 5 hours; check 74 °C at the center of the filling and firm masa.

r-mxc-tortas-ahogadas.summary: A savory birote roll filled with carnitas and drowned in a tomato sauce with very spicy chile de árbol.
r-mxc-tortas-ahogadas.history: A street-food icon of Guadalajara; the crusty birote holds up to the sauce without falling apart and is served with onion cured in lime.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons vinegar and salt to taste
steps: Blend the cooked tomatoes with garlic and spices and strain for the base sauce.
Grind the toasted chiles de árbol with vinegar and salt for the spicy salsa.
Cure the onion in lime juice with salt and oregano.
Slit the birotes open and fill them with carnitas.
Bathe the torta with the tomato sauce and add chile de árbol salsa to taste.
Top with the cured onion and serve right away.
tips: Serve hot chile sauce separately so everyone can adjust the heat without changing the tomato sauce.

r-mxc-carne-en-su-jugo.dishName: Carne en su jugo (beef in its juices)
r-mxc-carne-en-su-jugo.summary: Finely chopped steak cooked in its own broth with bayo beans, bacon, and green salsa.
r-mxc-carne-en-su-jugo.history: A Guadalajara specialty served in a clay bowl; it combines the meat in a light tomatillo broth with beans and fresh garnishes.
ingredients: Onion, cilantro, and lime to serve
steps: Brown the bacon in the pot until it renders its fat.
Add the chopped meat and sear it, stirring constantly.
Blend the tomatillos with serrano and garlic and pour over the meat.
Cook over medium heat until the meat is tender in its juices.
Serve with hot bayo beans.
Finish with onion, cilantro, and lime to taste.
tips: Add 250 ml water if the sauce does not provide enough liquid to gently cook the beef.

r-mxc-pescado-zarandeado.summary: Fish butterflied open, coated with adobo, and grilled over coals on a rack of branches.
r-mxc-pescado-zarandeado.history: A coastal preparation from Nayarit, tied to the island of Mexcaltitán; the fish is marinated and grilled slowly over charcoal for a smoky flavor.
steps: Make an adobo by blending guajillo, garlic, orange juice, and soy sauce.
Coat the butterflied fish with the adobo on both sides and let it marinate.
Place the fish on the rack or grill over the coals.
Grill the skin side first and flip carefully.
Cook until the flesh flakes off easily.
Serve with onion, tomato, lime, and tortillas to make tacos.
tips: Drain excess marinade before grilling and check 63 °C in the thickest fish section.

r-mxc-sopitos-colima.summary: Small fried masa cakes topped with ground beef and bathed in a light tomato-and-oregano sauce.
r-mxc-sopitos-colima.history: A classic snack from the supper stalls of Colima and Villa de Álvarez; it stands out for the tomato-and-oregano sauce it's generously bathed in.
steps: Form small sopitos with a raised rim and cook them on a griddle.
Cook the ground beef with salt and finely crumble it.
Blend the tomato with garlic and season with oregano for the sauce.
Dip each sopito in the sauce and fry it in lard on both sides.
Top with the beef and bathe with more sauce.
Finish with chopped onion and aged cheese.
tips: Cook ground beef to 71 °C and finish the sopitos at serving time to keep their bases firm.

r-mxc-carnitas.summary: Pork slowly confited in its own lard in a copper pot until tender inside and golden outside.
r-mxc-carnitas.history: The pride of Michoacán, especially Quiroga and Uruapan; the copper pot and long cooking in lard give carnitas their characteristic texture.
steps: Melt the lard in the copper pot over medium heat.
Add the pork pieces along with garlic, bay leaf, and salt.
Add the orange and a splash of milk to brown and tenderize.
Cook over low heat, stirring now and then, for a couple of hours.
Raise the heat at the end so the carnitas brown.
Chop and serve in tacos with onion, cilantro, and salsa.
tips: Add liquids carefully while the fat is still lukewarm; water added to very hot fat can splatter violently.

r-mxc-corundas.summary: A triangular tamal of masa wrapped in a corn-plant leaf, served with crema, salsa, and cheese.
r-mxc-corundas.history: A Purépecha tamal from Michoacán with its characteristic triangular shape; it's wrapped in the long leaf of the corn plant rather than in the dried husk.
ingredients: Long green leaves from the corn plant
Crema, red salsa, and cheese to serve
steps: Beat the lard until fluffy and work in the masa with salt and baking powder.
Place a portion of masa on the green leaf.
Fold the leaf at angles to form the characteristic triangle.
Steam the corundas for about an hour.
Let them rest a few minutes before unwrapping.
Serve bathed with crema, red salsa, and cheese.
tips: Keep boiling water below the rack without touching the parcels and top up with hot water as needed.

r-mxc-barbacoa.summary: Mutton slowly cooked in an earth oven, wrapped in maguey leaves until tender and juicy.
r-mxc-barbacoa.history: A Sunday tradition of central Mexico, deeply rooted in the State of Mexico and Hidalgo; it's cooked in a pit lined with maguey leaves.
ingredients: Guajillo and ancho chiles for the adobo
Chickpeas and rice for the consommé (optional)
steps: Coat the meat with an adobo of chiles, garlic, and spices.
Line the earth oven or a large pot with the maguey leaves.
Set a container underneath to catch the juices and make the consommé.
Arrange the meat on the leaves and cover it completely.
Cook for several hours over low heat until the meat shreds.
Serve in tacos with the consommé on the side, onion, cilantro, and salsa.
tips: For an oven version, cook well covered at 150-160 °C until the lamb shreds and retain the broth liquid.
sources: Cocina tradicional del centro de México

r-mxc-tacos-canasta.summary: Soft tacos of simple fillings, pressed and steamed in a basket, served hot and greasy.
r-mxc-tacos-canasta.history: Also called steamed or 'sweated' tacos; they're carried in wicker baskets through the streets of Mexico City and are tied in origin to Tlaxcala.
steps: Prepare the fillings separately and keep them warm.
Fill each tortilla with a filling and fold it.
Brush the tacos with the guajillo oil.
Layer them inside the cloth-lined basket.
Cover them well so they sweat and heat up with their own steam.
Serve with more green salsa, onion, and cilantro.
tips: Fillings must be fully cooked and hot when assembling; prepare only what will be served soon.
sources: Cocina callejera de la Ciudad de México

r-mxc-quesadillas-cdmx.summary: Folded masa tortillas with fillings and — depending on Mexico City taste — with or without cheese.
r-mxc-quesadillas-cdmx.history: An everyday craving in Mexico City; famous for the endless debate over whether a quesadilla comes with cheese or not when you order one at a stall.
ingredients: Fillings: squash blossom, huitlacoche, or mushrooms
steps: Form tortillas from the masa and place them on the griddle.
Add the filling and, if desired, the cheese and a leaf of epazote.
Fold the tortilla in half, pressing the edges.
Cook on both sides until the masa browns and the filling is hot.
Serve immediately with salsa to taste.
tips: Use already cooked and drained mushrooms or squash blossoms so they do not wet the dough.

r-mxc-pastes.summary: Flaky pastry turnovers filled with potato and meat, a legacy of the Cornish miners of England.
r-mxc-pastes.history: A Mexican adaptation of the Cornish pasty, brought to the mines of Real del Monte, Hidalgo, in the 19th century; today the fillings range from savory to sweet.
ingredients: 150 ml cold water, adjusted as needed
steps: Make a shortcrust dough with flour, cold fat, salt, and water; let it rest.
Mix the raw potato, meat, leek, and parsley with salt and pepper.
Roll out the dough and cut circles.
Add the filling, fold, and seal with the characteristic crimp.
Brush with egg and bake at 190 °C for 30-35 minutes, until golden and the filling reaches 71 °C; the potatoes must be tender.
Let cool slightly before serving.
tips: Dice potatoes about 5 mm thick so they cook alongside the meat inside the pastry.
sources: Cocina de Real del Monte, Hidalgo

r-mxc-cecina-yecapixtla.summary: A thin sheet of salted, air-dried beef, grilled over charcoal and served with crema, cheese, and guacamole.
r-mxc-cecina-yecapixtla.history: A specialty of the town of Yecapixtla, Morelos, famous for its thin beef cecina; it's served alongside chile-rubbed pork cecina and fresh garnishes.
steps: Grill the cecina over charcoal for a few seconds per side, taking care it doesn't dry out.
Grill the nopales and onion alongside the meat if you like.
Make a simple guacamole with avocado, cilantro, lime, and salt.
Serve the cecina with crema, cheese, and the guacamole.
Serve with warm tortillas to make tacos.
tips: Cecina already contains salt: taste the accompaniments before salting and check doneness with a thermometer.

r-mxc-mixiotes.summary: Chicken in a chile adobo steamed inside small parcels, traditionally made from maguey skin.
r-mxc-mixiotes.history: A dish of the central highlands, very present in Tlaxcala; the name comes from the thin film of the maguey plant in which the seasoned meat was originally wrapped.
steps: Rehydrate the chiles and blend them with garlic and spices for the adobo.
Marinate the chicken in the adobo for at least half an hour.
Place portions of chicken with an avocado leaf in each wrapper.
Close the mixiotes into small bundles.
Steam until the meat is tender.
Serve the mixiotes closed, to be opened at the table with tortillas.
tips: Always marinate in the refrigerator and check 74 °C in the thickest chicken piece.

r-pm-c-charales-fritos.summary: Tiny lake fish fried until crisp and golden, served in a paper cone with lime and salsa.
r-pm-c-charales-fritos.history: A delicacy of the Purépecha lake region, charales have been caught in Lake Pátzcuaro since pre-Hispanic times. They are sold hot at the docks and lakeside stands, wrapped in paper, as an emblematic snack of the town.
ingredients: 300 g dried or fresh cleaned charales (small lake fish)
Chile de árbol salsa for serving
steps: Rinse the charales and drain them very well; if dried, soak them for a few minutes and pat dry.
Sprinkle with lime juice and a little salt and let rest for 5 minutes.
Heat plenty of oil and fry the charales in batches until golden and crisp.
Drain them on paper towels to remove excess grease.
Serve hot in a paper cone with more lime and chile de árbol salsa.
tips: Dry the fish thoroughly after adding lime to reduce splattering during frying.
sources: México Desconocido, cocina lacustre de Pátzcuaro

r-pm-c-churipo.summary: A Purépecha red beef broth with guajillo chiles and vegetables, traditionally served with corundas.
r-pm-c-churipo.history: Churipo (from the Purépecha churhípu, 'broth') is a ceremonial stew of the highlands and the shores of Lake Pátzcuaro, deeply rooted in Tzintzuntzan. It is part of traditional Michoacán cuisine, recognized as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
ingredients: 1.2 kg beef shank or short rib
2 ears of corn, cut into pieces
steps: Cook the meat with onion, garlic, and salt until tender; reserve the broth.
Rehydrate the chiles and blend them with a little broth, garlic, and onion; strain.
Stir the strained sauce into the broth and let it simmer to develop flavor.
Add the corn, chayote, and cabbage and cook until tender.
Adjust the salt and add chopped xoconostle or a few drops of lime.
Serve piping hot, accompanied by corundas and tortillas.
tips: Add corn first, then chayote and finally cabbage so the cabbage does not fall apart.
sources: Cocina tradicional purépecha, El Sol de Morelia

r-pm-c-cantaritos.summary: A refreshing tequila cocktail with citrus juices and grapefruit soda, served in a clay pot.
r-pm-c-cantaritos.history: Born in the Amatitán and Tequila region in the early 20th century, cantaritos take their name from the small clay pot that keeps the drink cold and lends it a mineral note. Today they are a festive icon of the Magical Town of Tequila.
steps: Rim the clay pot with lime and chili salt.
Fill the pot with ice.
Pour in the tequila and the orange, lime, and grapefruit juices.
Top off with grapefruit soda and stir gently.
Garnish with citrus slices and serve immediately.
tips: Use a glazed clay mug certified food-safe and ice made from drinking water.

r-pm-c-el-bote.summary: A country three-meat broth cooked with pulque and vegetables, with a smoky flavor from the wood fire.
r-pm-c-el-bote.history: An emblematic dish of the Magical Town of Mazamitla, in the Jalisco highlands. Its name comes from the bote, or large pot, in which it was cooked over a wood fire; the pulque gives this festive stew its unique character.
ingredients: Onion, garlic, bay leaf, and salt
steps: In a large pot, sear the beef and pork with onion and garlic.
Cover with water, add bay leaf and salt, and cook until they begin to soften.
Add the chicken pieces and the vegetables cut into large chunks.
Pour in the pulque and add the whole chiles; cook over low heat.
Let everything cook slowly until the meats are very tender.
Serve the broth with the meats and vegetables, accompanied by tortillas and salsa.
tips: Add enough water to cover the meat and check that every chicken piece reaches 74 °C.
sources: Gastronomía del Pueblo Mágico de Mazamitla

r-pm-c-borrego-al-pastor.summary: Lamb marinated and slow-cooked in a clay oven or over coals, with a smoky flavor and tender meat.
r-pm-c-borrego-al-pastor.history: In Tapalpa, the tradition of borrego al pastor dates back to the Cristero War era, when those who took refuge in the sierra made use of firewood and lambs. It is cooked slowly and served with frijoles charros, distinct from pit barbacoa.
steps: Rehydrate the chiles and blend them with garlic, onion, spices, vinegar, and orange juice.
Coat the meat with the adobo and let it marinate several hours or overnight.
Arrange the lamb on a tray with avocado leaves and bay leaf.
Cook slowly, covered, in a clay oven or over coals until the meat falls apart.
Reserve the juices it releases to baste the meat when serving.
Serve with frijoles charros, onion, cilantro, and warm tortillas.
tips: In a home oven, cook covered at 160 °C and add some water to the base if the juices reduce too far.
sources: Latitud México, borrego al pastor de Tapalpa

r-pm-c-nieve-aguacate.summary: A creamy, unusually flavored churned ice: avocado blended with water, sugar, and lime.
r-pm-c-nieve-aguacate.history: Dolores Hidalgo is famous for its churned ices (nieves de garrafa) in extravagant flavors—avocado, mole, chicharrón, shrimp—sold at the stands around the main plaza. The avocado one is among the most beloved of this multi-generational ice-making tradition.
ingredients: Ice and rock salt for the churn
steps: Blend the avocado pulp with the water, sugar, and lime juice until smooth.
Pour the mixture into the churn canister (or a metal container).
Surround the canister with ice and rock salt so it chills below freezing.
Turn and scrape the mixture constantly to incorporate air and break up crystals.
Keep churning until you achieve a creamy, firm ice.
Serve immediately in a cup or cone.
tips: Keep salted ice outside the container holding the ice cream; do not let brine enter the mixture.
sources: México Desconocido, nieves de Dolores Hidalgo

r-pm-c-fiambre-san-miguel.summary: A cold salad of meats, fruits, and vegetables macerated in vinaigrette, typical of All Saints' Day.
r-pm-c-fiambre-san-miguel.history: San Miguel-style fiambre is prepared above all for November 1st. It combines chicken, tongue, and pig's feet with fruits and vegetables bathed in oil and vinegar; it is one of the most emblematic seasonal preparations of Guanajuato cuisine.
ingredients: Orange, banana, apple, jícama, and guava
Olive oil, vinegar, oregano, and salt
steps: Start with chicken, tongue and pork trotters already cooked and chilled in the refrigerator; this recipe describes assembling the cold platter.
Cut the fruits and vegetables into cubes or slices.
Prepare a vinaigrette with olive oil, vinegar, oregano, and salt.
Lay down a bed of lettuce and arrange the meats, fruits, and beet on top.
Bathe everything with the vinaigrette and let it macerate in the cold for at least an hour.
Serve garnished with avocado and olives.
tips: Chill cooked meats in the refrigerator and assemble cold; do not cool them on the counter for hours.
sources: Guanajuato.mx, fiambre estilo San Miguel de Allende

r-pm-c-gorditas-migajas.summary: Hand-ground corn gorditas stuffed with chicharrón bits and bathed in red salsa.
r-pm-c-gorditas-migajas.history: A signature street snack of the Magical Town of Bernal. They are made with hand-ground corn—white or blue—which makes them light and crisp, and filled with the migajas or 'achicalado' left over from making carnitas. They have more than half a century of tradition.
ingredients: 500 g coarsely ground corn masa (white or blue)
Cheese, lettuce, and onion for serving
steps: Knead the coarsely ground corn with a little salt until it can be shaped.
Form thick gorditas and open them with your fingers to create a pocket.
Fill them with the chicharrón bits and close them.
Cook them on the griddle with a little lard until golden on both sides.
Open them again and bathe them with red salsa.
Serve with crumbled cheese, lettuce, and onion.
tips: Seal the masa around the filling and cook over medium heat so it does not burn before cooking through.
sources: Gourmet de México, gorditas de migajas

r-pm-c-lengua-mechada.summary: Beef tongue larded with bacon and vegetables, slow-cooked and enhanced with local white wine.
r-pm-c-lengua-mechada.history: Tequisquiapan, a land of cheese and wine, boasts one of the state's best larded tongues. The tongue is stuffed with strips of bacon and cooked slowly until tender, paired with the white wine produced in the area.
ingredients: Tomato, onion, and garlic for the sauce
steps: Cook the tongue with onion, garlic, and salt until you can remove the skin.
Lard the tongue by inserting strips of bacon, carrot, and garlic.
Brown it in oil and remove it; in the same pot, sauté tomato, onion, and garlic.
Return the tongue, add the white wine and the herbs.
Cook covered over low heat until the meat is very tender.
Slice and serve bathed in its sauce, accompanied by rice or vegetables.
tips: Peel the tongue while it is warm because the skin releases more easily than when cold.
sources: Querétaro Travel, la comida de Tequisquiapan
México Destinos, comida típica de Tequisquiapan

r-pm-c-gorditas-horno.summary: Masa gorditas baked in a wood-fired oven, filled with stews such as chicharrón or potato with chorizo.
r-pm-c-gorditas-horno.history: In the mining Magical Town of Real de Catorce, gorditas are baked in a clay or wood-fired oven, which gives them a unique flavor. Known as the 'ranch hamburger' of the San Luis Potosí highlands, they are filled with chicharrón, potato with chorizo, or house stews.
ingredients: Green or red salsa for serving
steps: Knead the masa with salt and a little lard until smooth.
Form thick gorditas and make a pocket in them for the filling.
Fill with stewed chicharrón, potato with chorizo, or beans.
Seal the gorditas well and flatten them slightly.
Bake them in a very hot wood-fired or conventional oven until golden.
Serve hot with salsa to taste.
tips: Bake around 220 °C for 20-25 minutes and use already cooked, well-drained fillings.
sources: El Universal San Luis, gorditas de horno
Atractivos Turísticos de México, Real de Catorce

r-pm-c-bocoles.summary: Thick corn masa gorditas with bean, browned on the griddle and filled with cheese or chicharrón.
r-pm-c-bocoles.history: Bocoles are an everyday snack in the Huasteca Potosina and very present in Xilitla. They are made with nixtamalized corn masa mixed with bean or lard, cooked on the griddle, and split open to fill with cheese, chicharrón, or regional stews.
ingredients: 1 cup cooked and mashed black beans
steps: Mix the masa with the mashed beans, a little lard, and salt.
Knead until combined and form thick balls.
Flatten each ball into the shape of a thick gordita.
Cook them on a hot griddle until golden on both sides.
Split them open along one side and fill them with cheese.
Serve hot, accompanied by salsa.
tips: Drain the beans before mashing so the dough keeps its shape on the griddle.

r-pm-c-itacates.summary: A triangular corn masa snack with cheese, browned on the griddle and filled with stews to taste.
r-pm-c-itacates.history: The itacate (from the Nahuatl ihtacatl, 'provisions for the road') is the signature snack of Tepoztlán. Its triangular shape was created so field workers could carry hot food; today it is a must-stop in the market and streets of the Magical Town.
ingredients: Fillings to taste: mushrooms, squash blossom, or rajas
Green or red salsa for serving
steps: Mix the masa with the grated cheese, a little lard, and salt.
Form a thick tortilla and fold the edges to give it a triangular shape.
Cook it on the griddle until golden on both sides.
Carefully split it open along one side.
Fill with stewed mushrooms, squash blossom, or rajas.
Serve hot with salsa to taste.
tips: Make evenly thick triangles and carefully open them when cooked but still warm.
sources: Excélsior, qué son los itacates de Tepoztlán

r-pm-c-trucha-valle-bravo.summary: Fresh locally farmed trout browned in plenty of golden garlic, butter, and lime.
r-pm-c-trucha-valle-bravo.history: Trout is an emblematic product of Valle de Bravo thanks to the region's fish farms. It is served fresh in the lakeside restaurants, and its most beloved preparation is al mojo de ajo (garlic style), simple and aromatic.
steps: Season the trout inside and out with salt and pepper.
Brown the sliced garlic in butter and oil over low heat, without burning it.
Remove part of the garlic and set aside.
In the same pan, cook the trout on both sides until the skin browns.
Bathe with the garlic mojo and the lime juice.
Serve with the golden garlic on top and chopped parsley.
tips: Remove garlic as soon as it browns so it does not become bitter while the fish finishes cooking.
sources: Cocina Delirante, platillos de Valle de Bravo
The Corner, la trucha de Valle de Bravo

r-pm-c-naranjete.summary: An artisanal liqueur of orange, cane alcohol, and vanilla, slowly macerated until aromatic.
r-pm-c-naranjete.history: Naranjete is the traditional artisanal drink of Huasca de Ocampo, Mexico's first Magical Town. It is made by macerating orange with cane alcohol and vanilla, and is offered as a typical digestif of the Hidalgo sierra.
ingredients: 750 ml commercial drinking aguardiente, 40% alcohol by volume
steps: Juice the oranges and reserve the juice and some peels without the white pith.
Dissolve the sugar or piloncillo in the orange juice by warming it slightly.
Let it cool and mix with the cane alcohol.
Add the split vanilla, the cinnamon, and the orange peels.
Pour into a clean lidded jar and refrigerate for 7 days. Strain, keep refrigerated and consume promptly; this is not shelf-stable.
Strain and serve as a digestif, cold or at room temperature.
tips: Use only commercial alcoholic drinks fit for consumption, never industrial alcohol or antiseptic.
sources: Hidalgo Travel, Huasca pueblo con sabor
Comida tradicional de Huasca de Ocampo

r-pm-c-tatemado-comala.summary: A pork stew slow-cooked in an adobo of dried chiles, spices, and vinegar, with a deep, smoky flavor.
r-pm-c-tatemado-comala.history: Tatemado is an emblematic dish of Colima, and in the Magical Town of Comala it is prepared true to tradition. The pork is cooked slowly in a mixture of dried chiles, spices, and vinegar, achieving a concentrated and slightly smoky flavor.
steps: Rehydrate the chiles and blend them with garlic, spices, vinegar, and a little water; strain.
Marinate the pork in the adobo for at least an hour.
Place the meat with all the adobo in a pot with bay leaf and piloncillo.
Cook covered over low heat, stirring occasionally.
Let the meat cook until tender and the sauce thickens.
Serve with tortillas and rice or beans.
tips: Check the base every 20 minutes and add hot water if the marinade sticks before the meat softens.
sources: México Ruta Mágica, platillos típicos de Colima

r-pm-s-sopa-de-pan-coleta.dishName: Sopa de Pan Coleta (Coleto Bread Soup)
r-pm-s-sopa-de-pan-coleta.summary: A festive dish of toasted coleto bread slices, vegetables, egg, and fried plantain, bathed in a saffron-spiced broth.
r-pm-s-sopa-de-pan-coleta.history: A colonial-era recipe from San Cristóbal de las Casas, born as a Lenten dish in the 17th century. It combines the local coleto bread with ingredients brought by the Spanish, such as wine and saffron, and today it is served at civil and religious celebrations in the Chiapas highlands.
ingredients: 1 large loaf of coleto bread or a sliced and toasted baguette
Raisins, thyme, bay leaf, and chicken broth
steps: Toast the bread slices in the oven or on the griddle.
Prepare a broth with tomato, onion, saffron, and aromatic herbs.
Cook the carrot and zucchini separately.
In a casserole, layer the bread, vegetables, egg, and plantain.
Bathe with the hot broth and add raisins.
Let it rest a few minutes so the bread absorbs the broth, then serve.
tips: Toast bread thoroughly so it absorbs broth without immediately falling apart.

r-pm-s-pepita-con-tasajo.summary: A ceremonial dish of dried beef tasajo bathed in a thick sauce of squash seed, ground rice, and achiote.
r-pm-s-pepita-con-tasajo.history: It is the 'Comida Grande' (Great Meal) of the Fiesta Grande of Chiapa de Corzo, held January 4-23 and inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Its preparation begins at midnight, following rituals passed down through generations of cooks.
steps: Soak the tasajo to remove excess salt and lightly grill it.
Toast the squash seeds and the rice separately, then grind them finely.
Dilute the ground squash seeds and rice in water with achiote, tomato, and garlic.
Cook the sauce over low heat, stirring constantly so it does not break.
Add the tasajo in pieces and the avocado leaves.
Cook until it thickens and serve piping hot with tortillas.
tips: Taste the soaked tasajo before salting the sauce and add water if it becomes too thick.

r-pm-s-comiteco.summary: An ancestral spirit distilled from the aguamiel of the comiteco maguey, an element of cultural identity in Comitán de Domínguez.
r-pm-s-comiteco.history: Unlike other agave spirits, comiteco is made from the sap extracted from the heart of the living maguey, fermented and then distilled. In the 18th century it was considered the finest spirit in New Spain, and today it is undergoing a revival in Comitán, Chiapas.
ingredients: Grapefruit soda for making a cocktail (optional)
steps: Chill the glasses or shot glasses.
Serve the comiteco neat, straight up, to appreciate its agave aroma.
Accompany with citrus slices and a little worm salt.
For a cocktail, mix with ice and grapefruit soda.
Toast as is traditionally done at Comitán celebrations.
tips: This recipe uses a prepared commercial comiteco spirit; it does not include home fermentation or distillation.

r-pm-s-tlayoyos.summary: Oval corn masa gorditas filled with field pea or bean, cooked on the griddle and topped with salsa, cheese, and onion.
r-pm-s-tlayoyos.history: A snack of pre-Hispanic origin typical of the northeastern sierra of Puebla, including the Magical Town of Cuetzalan. Its name derives from Nahuatl, and its filling of ground field pea distinguishes it from the tlacoyos of central Mexico.
ingredients: 1 cup already cooked and mashed field peas
steps: Heat the already cooked, mashed peas and season with avocado leaf and salt.
Form thick masa tortillas and place the filling in the center.
Close and shape into an oval, flattening slightly.
Cook on a hot griddle on both sides until golden.
Top with salsa to taste.
Sprinkle with cheese and onion before serving.
tips: Use thick, cool or lukewarm filling so the masa can close without tearing.

r-pm-s-sidra-zacatlan.summary: A home adaptation of apple cider fermented with cider yeast and served without bottle carbonation.
r-pm-s-sidra-zacatlan.history: Zacatlán is known for apples and cider. This simplified home version does not reproduce a local commercial formula.
ingredients: 2 liters pasteurized apple juice, without preservatives that prevent fermentation
Cider yeast at the manufacturer’s dosage for 2 liters
steps: Clean and sanitize food-safe equipment following the sanitizer’s instructions.
Pour juice into a fermenter with headspace and add yeast according to its package.
Fit an airlock and ferment at the yeast manufacturer’s recommended temperature. Never seal the vessel airtight.
Use a hydrometer to confirm stable density over several days; 14 days is only a guide and fermentation may take longer.
Transfer without disturbing sediment, refrigerate and serve as still cider. This recipe includes neither priming sugar nor secondary bottle fermentation.
tips: Use clean food-safe equipment and a fermenter with an airlock; never seal active fermentation airtight.
sources: El Universal - Zacatlán de las Manzanas
Gourmet de México - Sidra de Zacatlán

r-pm-s-cecina-atlixco.summary: A thin sheet of salted, sun-dried beef, charcoal-grilled and served with nopales, cheese, avocado, and handmade tortillas.
r-pm-s-cecina-atlixco.history: The making of cecina in Atlixco dates back some 200 years, when fine beef cuts were salted and sun-dried. Today it is the culinary standard-bearer of the Magical Town and has its own Cecina Fair.
ingredients: Pickled chiles and pico de gallo
steps: Let the cecina come to room temperature for a few minutes.
Grill the cecina over charcoal or on the griddle for just a few seconds per side.
Grill the previously salted nopales.
Serve the cecina with nopales, cheese, and avocado.
Accompany with pickled chiles and pico de gallo.
Offer warm tortillas and crema for making tacos.
tips: Cook cecina to at least 63 °C and rest 3 minutes; do not rely on only a few seconds per side.

r-pm-s-cafe-coatepec.summary: A cup of high-altitude coffee grown in Coatepec, Mexico's coffee capital, with an intense aroma and balanced acidity.
r-pm-s-cafe-coatepec.history: Coatepec has produced coffee since 1808, when an arabica coffee seed arrived from Cuba at the Hacienda de Zimpizahua. Its altitude and climate at the foot of the Cofre de Perote earned it fame as the coffee capital of Mexico.
ingredients: 500 ml water at just below boiling
steps: Grind the coffee beans just before brewing.
Heat the water without letting it come to a full boil.
Pour the water over the coffee in a press or drip maker.
Let it steep for three to four minutes.
Serve in a cup, appreciating its aroma.
Sweeten with piloncillo if you like.
tips: For a French press, use coarse grounds and steep 4 minutes; for filter coffee, let water pass through without excessive stirring.

r-pm-s-mole-xiqueno.summary: A sweet, velvety mole from the Magical Town of Xico, made with more than twenty ingredients including chiles, dried fruits, cacao, and spices.
r-pm-s-mole-xiqueno.history: Mole de Xico, or mole xiqueño, is one of the most representative dishes of Veracruz cuisine. Its preparation can take more than two days and stands out for being sweeter than other dark moles thanks to the use of fruits such as prunes and plantain.
steps: Toast and soak the cleaned, seeded chiles.
Fry the dried fruits, seeds, plantain, and tortilla.
Grind everything with the chiles and spices into a paste.
Fry the paste in a casserole and add broth little by little.
Stir in the chocolate and cook over low heat until it thickens.
Bathe the cooked chicken pieces and serve with sesame seeds.
tips: Toast chiles for seconds and fry fruits separately to control browning.

r-pm-s-zacahuil.summary: A giant tamal of coarsely ground masa, chile adobo, and pork or turkey, wrapped in banana leaves and baked.
r-pm-s-zacahuil.history: An emblematic dish of the Totonacapan and the Huasteca, prepared in Papantla and other towns of northern Veracruz. With pre-Hispanic roots, it is a sign of hospitality: a single zacahuil can reach several meters and feed dozens of people at festivals and wakes.
ingredients: 1.5 kg pork and turkey, cut into pieces
steps: Prepare an adobo by grinding the chiles with garlic and spices.
Mix the coarsely ground masa with lard and part of the adobo.
Marinate the raw meat in the rest of the adobo.
Spread the masa over banana leaves and place the meat on top.
Wrap it into a large tamal and tie it well.
Bake over low heat for several hours until the meat is tender.
tips: Bake covered around 160 °C and check 74 °C at the center, especially when using turkey.

r-pm-s-arroz-a-la-tumbada.summary: A soupy tomato rice perfumed with epazote and loaded with seafood and fish from the Veracruz Sotavento.
r-pm-s-arroz-a-la-tumbada.history: A traditional dish of the Veracruz Sotavento, a region that includes Tlacotalpan and Alvarado. It is cooked in a single pot with the fresh catch of the day, and its soupy consistency distinguishes it from a dry rice.
ingredients: 200 g already cooked octopus, cut into pieces
1.5 liters hot fish stock, 2 epazote sprigs and salt
steps: Sauté the rice in oil until it becomes translucent.
Add the blended tomato, onion, and garlic.
Pour in plenty of fish broth so it stays soupy.
Add fish when the rice needs about 8 more minutes; add shrimp and already cooked octopus toward the end. Fish must reach 63 °C and shrimp must be opaque.
Add epazote and adjust the salt.
Cook until the rice is tender but still soupy and serve immediately.
tips: Keep extra stock hot: this rice should be soupy when served and will continue absorbing liquid.
sources: Larousse Cocina - Arroz a la tumbada
Jarochos en Línea - Gastronomía del Sotavento

r-pm-s-lomitos-valladolid.summary: Pieces of pork loin stewed in a thick tomato sauce with habanero, served with hard-boiled egg and ibes beans.
r-pm-s-lomitos-valladolid.history: An ancestral dish originating in the city of Valladolid, Yucatán. Its hallmark is slow cooking until the tomato reduces to a thick sauce; it is served with hard-boiled egg, ibes beans, and a whole habanero chile.
ingredients: Hard-boiled eggs and ibes beans for serving
steps: Brown the pork loin with salt, pepper, and onion in lard.
Blend the tomato with garlic and oregano.
Add the sauce to the meat along with the whole habanero chile.
Cook over low heat until the tomato reduces to a thick paste.
Adjust the seasoning without breaking the habanero.
Serve with sliced hard-boiled egg, ibes beans, and tortillas.
tips: Keep the habanero whole for aroma with less heat; avoid breaking it while stirring.

r-pm-s-relleno-negro.summary: A turkey or pork stew in a dark broth of recado negro, with ground-meat 'but' meatballs and hard-boiled egg.
r-pm-s-relleno-negro.history: An ancestral stew of the Yucatán Peninsula that blends Maya cooking with Spanish influences. Its characteristic color comes from recado negro, made of burnt chiles and tortillas. In Izamal, the Yellow Town, it remains alive in traditional kitchens.
ingredients: 1 turkey or 1.5 kg pork, in pieces
500 g ground meat for the 'but' meatballs
steps: Dissolve the recado negro in broth with tomato, garlic, and epazote.
Cook the turkey or pork in that dark broth.
Prepare the 'but' meatballs with ground meat and a little masa.
Add the meatballs to the stew so they cook through.
Stir in the hard-boiled eggs toward the end.
Serve with tortillas and habanero chile.
tips: Meatballs must reach 71 °C and turkey 74 °C; the dark broth is not a doneness indicator.

r-pm-s-salsa-de-jumiles.summary: A molcajete salsa of tomato and chile with live or toasted jumiles, cinnamon-flavored insects typical of Taxco.
r-pm-s-salsa-de-jumiles.history: Jumiles are an emblematic dish of Taxco, Guerrero, celebrated each year at the Jumil Fair in October. Their flavor recalls cinnamon because the insect feeds on oak leaves; they are eaten alive, ground with salt in a molcajete, or in salsa for tacos.
steps: Grill the tomatoes, chiles, and garlic on the griddle.
Use jumiles from a food supplier and cook them thoroughly on a griddle; this preparation does not use live insects.
Grind everything in a molcajete into a coarse salsa.
Adjust the salt.
Serve in the molcajete.
Accompany with freshly made tortillas to make tacos.
tips: Do not collect insects from pesticide-treated areas; use only food-grade products.
sources: México Travel Club - Salsa de jumiles
Viajero M - Feria del Jumil en Taxco

r-pm-s-trucha-capulalpam.summary: Farm-raised trout from the Sierra Juárez, grilled or in garlic mojo, served with regional herbs.
r-pm-s-trucha-capulalpam.history: In Capulálpam de Méndez, a Magical Town nestled in the coniferous forests of Oaxaca's Sierra Juárez, local ecotourism cooperatives raise trout in the rivers and serve it fresh, making it the dish most associated with the town.
steps: Season the trout with salt, lime, and herbs inside and out.
Prepare a mojo by browning the garlic in oil or butter.
Bathe the trout with the garlic mojo.
Grill or cook in a pan on both sides.
Cook until the flesh flakes easily.
Serve with a sierra-style side and tortillas.
tips: Use identified culinary herbs and check 63 °C at the center of the fish.

r-pm-s-rice-and-beans-bacalar.summary: Rice cooked with beans and coconut milk, an Afro-Caribbean side dish very present in Bacalar cuisine.
r-pm-s-rice-and-beans-bacalar.history: Bacalar's cuisine combines Yucatecan recipes with the Belizean cooking of southern Quintana Roo. Rice and beans—rice and beans cooked in coconut milk—reflects this Afro-Caribbean heritage and is served alongside fish and lagoon stews.
ingredients: 1 cup coconut milk and 2 cups bean cooking liquid or water
steps: Sauté the garlic and onion in a little oil.
Add cooked beans and the 2 cups of cooking liquid or water; bring to a gentle boil.
Stir in the rice and the coconut milk.
Season with thyme, pepper, and salt.
Cook covered over low heat until the rice absorbs the liquid.
Fluff with a fork and serve as a side dish.
tips: Rest covered for 10 minutes after turning off the heat and fluff with a fork without crushing the beans.
sources: Mexican Caribbean - La gastronomía de Bacalar
Casa Bakal - Qué comer en Bacalar

r-pm-s-pampano-escabeche.summary: Pompano fish cooked and marinated in an escabeche of vinegar, onion, garlic, and spices, typical of Campeche riverside cooking.
r-pm-s-pampano-escabeche.history: In the Magical Town of Palizada, bathed by the river of the same name, Campeche cuisine makes use of the fresh fish from its waters. Pámpano en escabeche is a traditional preparation of the region that preserves the fish in a tart marinade of vinegar and spices.
steps: Season the pompano with salt and lightly sear it in oil.
Remove the fish and, in the same oil, sauté onion and garlic.
Add the vinegar, bay leaf, thyme, and allspice.
Let it come to a boil to form the escabeche.
Return the fish and cook a few minutes in the marinade.
Serve warm or refrigerate in a shallow container once it stops steaming. Vinegar does not make this fish safe for storage outside the refrigerator.
tips: Cook fish to 63 °C before cooling and always keep the escabeche refrigerated.
sources: La Revista del Sureste - Gastronomía de Campeche

r-mxs-cochinita.summary: Pork marinated in achiote and sour orange juice, wrapped in banana leaves and cooked until it falls apart.
r-mxs-cochinita.history: A Maya legacy traditionally cooked in a pib, an underground oven. Achiote and sour orange are the signature of the Yucatán Peninsula, and today it is served in tortas, tacos, and panuchos.
ingredients: 1.5 kg pork leg, cut into chunks
Red onion and habanero chile for pickling
steps: Dissolve the achiote in the sour orange juice with garlic and spices.
Marinate the pork in the adobo for at least 4 hours or overnight.
Toast the banana leaves to make them pliable and line a baking dish.
Place the meat with its marinade, wrap, and cover tightly.
Bake at low heat until the meat shreds on its own.
Serve with red onion pickled in sour orange and habanero.
tips: Bake covered at 160 °C for about 3.5 hours; add hot water if the pan dries before the marinade burns.

r-mxs-sopa-lima.summary: An aromatic chicken or turkey broth perfumed with Yucatecan lima and topped with fried tortilla strips.
r-mxs-sopa-lima.history: A signature dish of Yucatecan cooking, made with the peninsula's sour lima, a citrus distinct from the common lime that gives it its unmistakable aroma.
ingredients: Corn tortillas cut into strips for frying
steps: Cook the chicken with onion and salt to make a clear broth.
Shred the chicken and set the strained broth aside.
Saute the onion, bell pepper, and tomato; add them to the broth.
Add the chicken and a few lima slices; let it boil briefly.
Fry the tortilla strips until golden.
Serve the broth with lima juice to taste and tortilla chips on top.
tips: Use about 1.5 liters water for the stock and add lime juice at the end to preserve its aroma.

r-mxs-panuchos.summary: A refried-bean-stuffed tortilla, fried and topped with cochinita or turkey, pickled onion, and avocado.
r-mxs-panuchos.history: A classic Yucatecan antojito sold in markets and lunch counters. The tortilla puffs up on the comal, is opened, and is filled with strained beans before frying.
ingredients: 300 g cochinita pibil or shredded turkey
Habanero chile and oil for frying
steps: Heat the tortillas until they puff and open them along one side.
Fill each tortilla with strained refried beans.
Fry the panuchos until crisp.
Top with the shredded meat.
Add pickled onion and avocado.
Serve with habanero chile salsa.
tips: Use thick beans and already cooked meat; excess liquid can split the tortilla during frying.

r-mxs-papadzules.summary: Hard-boiled egg tacos bathed in a pumpkin-seed sauce and seed oil, with tomato sauce.
r-mxs-papadzules.history: A dish of Maya roots whose name is often translated as 'food for the lords.' Its green pumpkin-seed sauce is its defining element within Yucatecan cooking.
ingredients: 4 epazote leaves and 500 ml vegetable stock or water
steps: Simmer the ground pumpkin seeds with broth and epazote until they form a thick sauce.
Reserve the green oil that the pumpkin seeds release.
Prepare a roasted tomato sauce with onion.
Dip the tortillas in the pumpkin-seed sauce and fill them with egg.
Roll the tacos and bathe them with more pumpkin-seed sauce.
Garnish with the tomato sauce and the pumpkin-seed oil.
tips: Grind pumpkin seeds finely and add stock gradually: the sauce should coat tortillas without becoming a dry paste.
sources: Diccionario enciclopédico de la gastronomía mexicana

r-mxs-pan-cazon.summary: Layers of tortilla, refried beans, and stewed dogfish, bathed in tomato sauce with habanero chile.
r-mxs-pan-cazon.history: An emblem of Campeche cooking, built like a tower of tortillas filled with shredded dogfish shark. It is the state's most representative dish.
steps: Stew the shredded dogfish with onion, tomato, and epazote.
Prepare a tomato sauce with habanero chile.
Spread a tortilla with beans and place dogfish on top.
Repeat in layers to build the tower.
Bathe it all with the hot tomato sauce.
Serve immediately with more habanero to taste.
tips: Drain the cooked fish mixture and assemble just before saucing so the layers hold their shape.

r-mxs-pozole-verde.summary: A cacahuazintle corn broth with pork or chicken and a green sauce of pumpkin seed, tomatillo, and chile.
r-mxs-pozole-verde.history: Green pozole is Guerrero's signature version, distinguished by the ground pumpkin seed that gives it color and body. It is traditionally served on Thursdays.
ingredients: Radish, oregano, and lime to serve
steps: Cook the corn with the meat until both are tender.
Toast and grind the pumpkin seeds with tomatillo, chile, and epazote.
Fry the pumpkin-seed sauce, taking care that it does not split.
Stir the sauce into the broth with corn and meat.
Cook over low heat until the flavors come together.
Serve with lettuce, radish, onion, oregano, and lime.
tips: Blend the cilantro and some listed lettuce into the sauce for color; reserve the rest for serving.

r-mxs-pescado-talla.dishName: Pescado a la talla (grilled chile-rubbed fish)
r-mxs-pescado-talla.summary: Fish butterflied open, rubbed with a chile adobo, and grilled over coals, typical of the Guerrero coast.
r-mxs-pescado-talla.history: A specialty of the Guerrero coast associated with Barra Vieja in Acapulco. The fish is marinated in a red chile adobo and grilled over charcoal.
ingredients: 1 red snapper or snook, butterflied open
