Mustard and mayonnaise for the crust
steps: Grind the soaked chiles with garlic, spices, and orange juice.
Butterfly the fish open and salt it.
Rub one side with red adobo and the other with green adobo or mustard.
Grill over the coals, starting with the skin side.
Flip carefully until the flesh is firm.
Serve with tortillas, grilled onion, and lime.
tips: This list supports a red-marinade and mustard coating; no extra green sauce is needed.

r-mxs-mole-amarillo.summary: A light stew of chilcostle and guajillo chiles thickened with masa, served with meat and vegetables.
r-mxs-mole-amarillo.history: One of Oaxaca's seven moles, known as amarillito. It stands out for the hoja santa and for being thickened with corn masa instead of seeds and nuts.
ingredients: Chilcostle, guajillo, and yellow costeno chiles
steps: Cook the meat and vegetables separately.
Toast and soak the chiles; grind them with tomato and garlic.
Fry the strained sauce in a pot.
Dissolve the masa in broth and add it to thicken.
Add the hoja santa and let it simmer over low heat.
Stir in the meat and vegetables; season and serve.
tips: Dissolve masa in cold stock first to thicken the sauce without lumps.

r-mxs-memelas.summary: Thick oval tortillas with a pinched rim, spread with pork lard, beans, and quesillo.
r-mxs-memelas.history: A breakfast antojito very popular in Oaxaca's markets. The masa is pinched around the edges to hold the pork drippings and salsa.
ingredients: Chile de arbol or pasilla salsa
steps: Form thick oval tortillas and pinch the edges.
Cook them on the comal on both sides.
Spread pork drippings over the hot memela.
Add refried beans and salsa to taste.
Sprinkle with shredded quesillo.
Return to the comal until the cheese melts.
tips: Pinch the edges while the masa is warm and flexible, before adding beans.
sources: Cocina de los Valles Centrales de Oaxaca

r-mxs-tejate.summary: A pre-Hispanic cold drink of corn and cacao crowned with a foam contributed by the cacao flower.
r-mxs-tejate.history: Called the drink of the gods, it is of Zapotec origin and was prepared in planting and harvest ceremonies. San Andres Huayapan is its main center of production.
ingredients: Cold water and sugar to taste
steps: Grind the corn with the cacao, cacao flower, and mamey pit into a paste.
Knead the paste, adding water little by little.
Work the mixture by hand until the foam rises.
Dilute in cold water inside a jicara gourd.
Sweeten to taste without breaking down the foam.
Serve well chilled, making sure to share out the foam.
tips: Use cooked corn and mamey kernel prepared for tejate by a food supplier; do not substitute raw seeds.

r-mxs-cochito.summary: Pork marinated in an ancho chile adobo, vinegar, and spices, baked until very tender.
r-mxs-cochito.history: A culinary treasure of Tuxtla Gutierrez and of Chiapas in general. It is prepared in wood-fired ovens for festivities and served in tacos or on a plate with lettuce.
ingredients: Lettuce and onion to serve alongside
steps: Grind the ancho chiles with vinegar, garlic, and spices.
Marinate the meat in the adobo and let it rest overnight.
Place the meat in a baking dish and add water to cover.
Bake covered at 170 °C for about 2 hours until the pork separates easily with a fork; uncover at the end if you want to brown it.
Baste the meat with its juices during cooking.
Serve with lettuce, onion, and tortillas.
tips: Marinate in the refrigerator and turn the meat once to distribute the seasoning.

r-mxs-tamales-chipilin.summary: Soft masa tamales with chipilin leaves, typical of Chiapas and Tabasco.
r-mxs-tamales-chipilin.history: Chipilin is an aromatic herb of the southeast that perfumes the masa. These small tamales are wrapped in banana leaf and sometimes include quesillo or pumpkin seed.
steps: Beat the masa with lard and broth until fluffy.
Fold in the cleaned chipilin leaves.
Toast the banana leaves and cut them into squares.
Place a portion of masa and a piece of quesillo.
Wrap the tamales into small packets.
Steam for about an hour.
tips: Tamales are ready when the masa releases from the leaf; rest 10 minutes after steaming.
sources: Diccionario enciclopédico de la gastronomía mexicana

r-mxs-pejelagarto.summary: A fish endemic to Tabasco, grilled over charcoal and served shredded with amashito chile.
r-mxs-pejelagarto.history: The pejelagarto is a prehistoric fish from the rivers and lagoons of Tabasco. It is grilled whole over coals, and its flesh is used in tacos with amashito chile salsa.
steps: Clean the pejelagarto and salt it inside.
Grill it whole over the coals, turning it little by little.
Remove the hard skin and pull off the flesh.
Shred the grilled flesh.
Prepare an amashito chile salsa with lime and onion.
Serve the meat in tacos with the salsa.
tips: Ask for cleaned fish and check 63 °C before removing the skin and separating the bones.

r-mxs-huachinango-ver.dishName: Huachinango a la veracruzana (Veracruz-style red snapper)
r-mxs-huachinango-ver.summary: Fillet or whole fish in a tomato sauce with olives, capers, and guero chiles.
r-mxs-huachinango-ver.history: A flagship dish of the port of Veracruz, born of the blend of Indigenous and Spanish cooking. The sauce combines tomato with olives, capers, and Mediterranean herbs.
ingredients: 1 whole red snapper or in fillets
Lime juice, parsley, and olive oil
steps: Marinate the fish with lime and salt.
Saute onion and garlic in olive oil.
Add the chopped tomato and cook until it forms a sauce.
Stir in olives, capers, guero chiles, and bay leaf.
Cook the fish in the sauce until it is firm.
Sprinkle with parsley and serve hot.
tips: Taste after adding capers and olives because they supply plenty of salt.

r-mxs-picadas.summary: Thick tortillas with a pinched rim, red or green salsa, onion, and fresh cheese.
r-mxs-picadas.history: A typical Veracruz breakfast served in diners and markets. The pinched rim holds the salsa that covers them, red or green depending on the house.
steps: Form thick tortillas and pinch the edges as they come off the comal.
Spread a little lard over the surface.
Cover each picada with red or green salsa.
Sprinkle with chopped onion.
Add crumbled fresh cheese.
Serve hot, freshly assembled.
tips: Pinch the tortilla as soon as it is cool enough to handle and finish with hot sauce.

r-mxs-tikin-xic.summary: Fish marinated in an achiote and sour orange recado, wrapped in banana leaves and grilled.
r-mxs-tikin-xic.history: A preparation of Maya origin popular on the coasts of Quintana Roo and Yucatán. Its name means dry fish, and today it is grilled wrapped in banana leaves.
ingredients: 1 grouper or red snapper, butterflied open
steps: Dissolve the achiote in sour orange juice.
Rub the opened fish with the recado and let it marinate.
Place slices of tomato, onion, and bell pepper on top.
Wrap the fish in toasted banana leaves.
Grill or cook on the comal on both sides.
Serve with tortillas and pickled onion.
tips: Use clean, flexible leaves and check 63 °C in the fish, opening the parcel carefully to avoid steam.
sources: Cocina maya de la península de Yucatán

r-mxs-mole-poblano.summary: A thick sauce of chiles, spices, nuts, and chocolate, served over turkey or chicken.
r-mxs-mole-poblano.history: One of Puebla's most celebrated dishes, traditionally attributed to the colonial convents. It combines Indigenous and European ingredients in a sauce of dozens of components.
steps: Toast and soak the chiles, taking care not to burn them.
Fry the nuts, raisins, bread, and plantain.
Grind the chiles and the other ingredients with spices.
Fry the ground paste in hot lard.
Add broth and the chocolate tablet; simmer over low heat.
Bathe the turkey or chicken pieces and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
tips: Start with 8 mulato, 4 ancho and 2 pasilla chiles; add stock gradually and avoid burning seeds when toasting.

r-mxs-tinga-poblana.summary: Shredded chicken stewed with tomato, onion, and chipotle, served over tostadas.
r-mxs-tinga-poblana.history: A simple Puebla stew served over tostadas or in tacos. Chipotle gives it its characteristic smoky, mildly spicy flavor.
steps: Saute the sliced onion until softened.
Add the blended tomato and cook until thickened.
Stir in the chopped chipotles with a little of their adobo.
Add the shredded chicken and let it season.
Serve the tinga over tostadas.
Top with cream, fresh cheese, and avocado.
tips: Add chipotle gradually and taste because heat varies considerably between brands.

r-pm-n-gallina-pinta.summary: A Sonoran broth of pinto beans, nixtamal corn, and beef short rib, with no hen at all despite its name.
r-pm-n-gallina-pinta.history: In Alamos, a colonial jewel of southern Sonora, this broth is a local emblem. It is said to have been born of the need to stretch a meal for large families and ranch laborers, uniting beans and corn of Indigenous roots with the beef of the cattle-raising north. Its name plays on the mottled tones the grains take on as they cook; it is sometimes called 'the poor man's pozole.'
ingredients: Cilantro and chopped onion to serve
steps: Soak the pinto beans overnight and drain them.
In a large pot, cook the short rib with half an onion and the garlic until it releases its flavor.
Add the beans and cook over medium heat until they begin to soften.
Stir in the nixtamal corn and keep cooking until beans and corn are tender and the broth takes on body.
Adjust the salt, add the green chiles if using, and let it boil a few more minutes.
Serve piping hot with cilantro, chopped onion, and flour tortillas.
tips: Raw and precooked corn need different cooking times; this version works best with already cooked hominy.
sources: Noro - La gallina pinta, tesoro gastronómico de Sonora

r-pm-n-coricos-de-mocorito.summary: Crunchy ring cookies of corn masa and piloncillo or sugar, a traditional cookie of northern Sinaloa.
r-pm-n-coricos-de-mocorito.history: Mocorito, nicknamed the 'Athens of Sinaloa' and a Pueblo Magico since 2015, keeps a very lively home-baking tradition. Among its wheat and corn sweets, the coricos stand out: baked masa rings that families make to go with coffee and that are sold in the town's bakeries alongside bizcotelas and empanadas.
ingredients: 2 cups corn masa (nixtamal masa or hydrated corn flour)
steps: Cream the lard with the sugar until smooth.
Add the egg and mix; fold in the corn masa, flour, salt, and cinnamon.
Knead until you get a workable dough that does not stick.
Take portions, form strips, and join them into a ring or hoop shape.
Arrange on a tray and bake at 180 C for about 18 to 20 minutes, until golden.
Let cool so they turn crunchy before serving.
tips: Cool the rings on a rack; they become crisp as they lose heat.

r-pm-n-pescado-zarandeado-mazatlan.summary: A whole fish butterflied open, marinated and grilled over coals on a mangrove rack called a zaranda.
r-pm-n-pescado-zarandeado-mazatlan.history: The zarandeado takes its name from the 'zaranda,' a grill woven from mangrove sticks that lets you turn the fish without breaking it. Although its origin is attributed to the Totorame area of Nayarit and Mexcaltitan, in the port of Mazatlan it became a regional specialty, served by the sea with tortillas and citrus salsas.
ingredients: 1 whole red snapper or snook (1.5 kg), butterflied open
Onion, tomato, and chile in slices to serve alongside
steps: Clean the fish and butterfly it open, keeping it joined along the back.
Mix soy sauce, lime juice, garlic, Worcestershire sauce, salt, and pepper; brush it over all the flesh.
If you want a golden crust, spread a light layer of mayonnaise on the flesh side.
Let it marinate for 15 to 20 minutes.
Grill over medium heat, first on the skin side and then the flesh side, until cooked and lightly browned.
Serve with the sliced vegetables, corn tortillas, and hot salsa.
tips: Soy and Worcestershire sauces already contain salt; taste before adding more.
sources: El Sol de Mazatlán - Pescado zarandeado, ¿de Mazatlán o Nayarit?

r-pm-n-trucha-de-la-sierra-tarahumara.summary: Fresh stream trout butterflied open and grilled with butter, herbs, and lime, a mountain dish of Creel.
r-pm-n-trucha-de-la-sierra-tarahumara.history: Creel, gateway to the Copper Canyon in the Sierra Tarahumara, makes use of trout raised in the streams and farms of the Chihuahua highlands. It is a simple mountain dish that reflects Raramuri cooking and the cold of the conifer forest where it is served freshly made.
ingredients: 2 fresh trout, cleaned and butterflied open
steps: Season the trout inside and out with salt and pepper.
Melt the butter with the garlic and herbs in a skillet or on a comal.
Place the trout flesh side down and cook until lightly browned.
Flip carefully and finish cooking on the skin side.
Drizzle with lime juice and the pan butter when serving.
Serve with potatoes or highland flour tortillas.
tips: Dry the fish before cooking and check 63 °C in its thickest part.
sources: Hotel Posada del Cobre - Gastronomía de Creel y Chihuahua
La Opción de Chihuahua - Platillos típicos de la Sierra Tarahumara

r-pm-n-pan-de-pulque-de-saltillo.summary: A fluffy wheat bread fermented with pulque, with a light tang and a scent of cinnamon.
r-pm-n-pan-de-pulque-de-saltillo.history: Pan de pulque is one of Saltillo's oldest baking traditions. It was born in the Tlaxcalan neighborhood of San Esteban de la Nueva Tlaxcala, when colonial bakers discovered that pulque, the fermented drink of the maguey, could serve as leavening for wheat. It is also known as pan de fiesta or pan mestizo, and several families have made it for generations.
steps: Mix part of the flour with the pulque to form a sponge and let it ferment in a warm place until it doubles in volume.
Separately, cream the butter with the sugar and add the eggs.
Combine the fermented sponge with the rest of the flour, the cinnamon, the salt, and the butter mixture.
Knead until you get a soft, elastic dough; let it rest until it rises again.
Shape the loaves, place them on a tray, and let them proof one last time.
Bake at 180 C for about 20 to 25 minutes, until golden.
tips: Pulque fermentation varies: judge by rising volume and allow at least 3 hours waiting time.
sources: Milenio - Historia del pan de pulque de Saltillo
Posta - Pan de pulque de Saltillo, un bocado de tradición

r-pm-n-cortadillo-de-cuatro-cienegas.summary: Chunks of beef stewed in a tomato, bell pepper, and onion broth, a northern dish of Cuatro Cienegas.
r-pm-n-cortadillo-de-cuatro-cienegas.history: In Cuatro Cienegas, a Pueblo Magico of Coahuila known for its crystal-clear water pools, cortadillo is everyday food. It is a humble stew of cooked beef, shredded or in small pieces, bathed in a tomato and bell pepper broth, served with flour tortillas and beans.
ingredients: 600 g beef for shredding (flank or chuck)
Salt, pepper, and cumin to taste
steps: Cook the beef with a piece of onion and garlic until tender; set it aside and cut into strips or shred it.
Blend the tomato with garlic and a little of the cooking broth.
Soften the onion and bell pepper, adding the chile if you use it.
Stir in the beef and saute for a couple of minutes.
Pour in the blended tomato, season with salt, pepper, and cumin, and let it boil until the broth thickens.
Serve hot with flour tortillas and refried beans.
tips: Flank may take longer than an hour to soften; add hot stock and continue until it shreds.
sources: Posta - Platillos especiales de Cuatro Ciénegas
Cocina Delirante - Platillos típicos de Cuatro Ciénegas

r-pm-n-glorias-de-linares.summary: A candy of burnt goat's-milk caramel with pecans, wrapped in its classic red cellophane, the pride of Linares.
r-pm-n-glorias-de-linares.history: Glorias were born in Linares, Nuevo Leon, around the 1930s, when Dona Natalia Medina sold blocks of pecan milk caramel. Legend says her customers described the flavor as 'a glory,' and the name stuck. Originally they were made with goat's milk, so typical of the northeast, and are wrapped in the recognizable red cellophane.
steps: In a heavy-bottomed pot, mix both milks with the sugar, cinnamon, and baking soda.
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly so it does not stick.
Keep cooking until the mixture thickens and takes on a golden caramel tone.
Remove the cinnamon and stir in the chopped pecans.
Let it cool a little and form small balls or little blocks.
Wrap each gloria in cellophane to keep it.
tips: Stir while scraping the base and test a cooled drop; it should form a soft, moldable piece.

r-pm-n-enchiladas-tultecas.summary: Red-tortilla enchiladas filled with cheese and chorizo, topped with lettuce, tomato, and chile piquin.
r-pm-n-enchiladas-tultecas.history: Tula, the first Pueblo Magico of Tamaulipas and home of the Tamaulipan cuera leather jacket, has in the enchiladas tultecas its most representative dish. The tortilla is dyed red with chile and filled with cheese and chorizo, served with fresh vegetables; they are eaten in nearly every eatery in town.
ingredients: 4 ancho or guajillo chiles for the salsa
1 garlic clove and salt to taste
steps: Rehydrate the chiles in hot water and blend them with garlic and salt to form a thick salsa.
Fry the chorizo until well cooked and set it aside.
Dip the tortillas in the chile salsa to dye them and fry them lightly.
Fill each tortilla with cheese, chorizo, and onion, and roll it up.
Arrange the enchiladas and bathe them with a little more salsa.
Serve with lettuce, tomato, and chile piquin sprinkled on top.
tips: Drain the cooked chorizo so the enchiladas do not become overly greasy.
sources: El Mañana - El Pueblo Mágico de Tula, Tamaulipas

r-pm-n-gorditas-de-horno-duranguenses.summary: Sweet baked flour or corn gorditas with piloncillo and cinnamon, a Durango baking tradition.
r-pm-n-gorditas-de-horno-duranguenses.history: Baked gorditas are a deeply rooted culinary tradition in Durango. The sweet ones, made with wheat flour, piloncillo or sugar, and lard, are cooked in a wood-fired oven and sold along the state's streets and highways, a typical treat to go with coffee.
ingredients: Milk, as needed to bring it together
steps: Mix the flour with the baking powder, cinnamon, and piloncillo.
Work in the shortening with your hands until you get a sandy texture.
Add the egg and milk little by little until a soft dough forms.
Roll out the dough and cut thick discs.
Place them on a tray and bake at 180 C for 20 to 25 minutes, until golden.
Let them cool slightly and serve with cafe de olla.
tips: Add milk a spoonful at a time and space the pieces apart for even browning.
sources: Posta - Gorditas de horno, tradición culinaria de Durango
Noro - Dulces y postres típicos de Durango

r-pm-n-enchiladas-zacatecanas.summary: Tortillas dipped in chile salsa, filled with cheese and onion, a classic Zacatecas street dish.
r-pm-n-enchiladas-zacatecanas.history: In the Zacatecas capital they are simply called 'enchiladas'; outside the state the demonym is added to signal their origin. They are famous during the Holy Week festivals, when long tables are set up next to the cathedral and the stalls make them to order in pork lard.
ingredients: 250 g crumbled fresh or asadero cheese
Pork lard or oil for frying
steps: Rehydrate the chiles and blend them with garlic, salt, and a little water to form the salsa.
Heat the lard in a skillet.
Dip each tortilla in the chile salsa and then fry it lightly.
Fill with cheese and onion and fold or roll it.
Arrange the enchiladas and bathe them with more hot salsa.
Serve immediately with lettuce and sprinkled cheese.
tips: Fry tortillas briefly so they remain flexible enough to fold without cracking.
sources: El Informador - Platillos típicos de Zacatecas

r-pm-n-langosta-estilo-puerto-nuevo.summary: Lobster split and fried in lard, served with flour tortillas, beans, rice, and butter with lime.
r-pm-n-langosta-estilo-puerto-nuevo.history: Puerto Nuevo, the 'lobster town' in the municipality of Playas de Rosarito, popularized this dish in the 1950s. The fishermen's wives opened their homes to cook the freshly caught lobster in lard and serve it with handmade flour tortillas; today more than twenty restaurants keep the tradition alive.
ingredients: Refried beans and rice to serve alongside
steps: Split the lobsters lengthwise and season them with salt and pepper.
Heat plenty of lard in a large skillet.
Fry the lobster halves flesh side down until they change color and stay juicy.
Melt the butter with lime juice for the mojo sauce.
Serve the lobster with the lime butter for dipping.
Serve with hot flour tortillas, beans, and rice.
tips: Lobster flesh must be firm and opaque throughout; shell color alone does not establish doneness.
sources: Gourmet de México - Historia de la langosta estilo Puerto Nuevo

r-pm-n-ceviche-de-marlin-ahumado.summary: A fresh ceviche made with smoked marlin, tomato, onion, and lime, a coastal specialty of Todos Santos.
r-pm-n-ceviche-de-marlin-ahumado.history: Todos Santos, a Pueblo Magico of Baja California Sur between La Paz and Cabo San Lucas, is famous for its seafood cooking. Smoked marlin, very typical of the peninsula, becomes a juicy, flavorful ceviche served on a tostada, one of the town's most sought-after treats.
steps: Flake the smoked marlin and remove any bones.
Mix the fish with the tomato, onion, and chile.
Add the lime juice and let it rest a few minutes to take on flavor.
Stir in the cilantro and adjust the salt and pepper.
Serve cold over tostadas.
Serve with hot salsa and avocado to taste.
tips: Use commercial smoked fish labeled ready to eat and keep refrigerated until mixing.
sources: Food and Pleasure - Pueblo Mágico Todos Santos
Noro - Qué comer en los pueblos mágicos de Baja California Sur

r-us-mw-chicago-deep-dish.summary: A tall, thick-crusted pan pizza with the cheese on the bottom, a generous filling, and tomato sauce on top, a Chicago trademark.
r-us-mw-chicago-deep-dish.history: It is credited to Pizzeria Uno in Chicago, where this deep version baked in a steel pan became popular in the late 1940s. Unlike Neapolitan pizza, the dough forms a kind of deep tart: first the cheese, then the toppings, and finally the sauce, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake. It became a culinary symbol of the city.
ingredients: 300 g thick tomato sauce with oregano and garlic
steps: Mix both flours, yeast, salt, water and butter; knead, cover and let rise 60 minutes until doubled.
Roll out the dough and line a greased deep pan, pressing it up the sides.
Cover the bottom with the mozzarella slices to protect it from the sauce.
Add the sausage or other toppings and finish with the tomato sauce on top.
Bake at 220°C for about 30 to 35 minutes until the edge turns golden.
Let rest a few minutes before cutting into deep slices.
tips: Use precooked, drained sausage to control the filling’s moisture.
sources: Historia de la pizza deep-dish de Chicago

r-us-mw-chicago-hot-dog.summary: An all-beef sausage on a poppy seed bun with seven classic toppings, always served without ketchup.
r-us-mw-chicago-hot-dog.history: It emerged in Chicago during the Great Depression as hearty, cheap street food, closely tied to Eastern European immigrant communities. The local rule is strict: never any ketchup. Its combination of mustard, green relish, onion, tomato, pickle, sport peppers, and celery salt is known as being 'dragged through the garden.'
steps: Heat the sausages by steaming or in hot water without letting them boil hard.
Warm the buns with steam so they turn soft.
Place the sausage and add mustard and relish lengthwise.
Add onion, tomato wedges, pickle and pickled peppers.
Finish with a pinch of celery salt and serve immediately, never with ketchup.
tips: Heat sausages without a strong boil to prevent split skins.
sources: Cultura del hot dog de Chicago
Historia de la comida callejera de Illinois

r-us-mw-italian-beef.summary: A sandwich of thinly sliced roast beef soaked in its own spiced jus and topped with giardiniera or sweet peppers.
r-us-mw-italian-beef.history: It was born in Chicago's Italian-American communities, where to stretch cheap cuts of beef they roasted them, sliced them very thin, and served them on bread dipped in the beef's own broth. It became popular at banquets and later in small shops around the city. You order it 'wet' or 'dipped' depending on how much jus it gets, with hot giardiniera or sweet green peppers.
ingredients: 1.5 kg beef round or eye of round
steps: Rub the meat with garlic, oregano, fennel, chile, salt, and pepper.
Roast it at 160°C until cooked but juicy; let cool to slice thin.
Heat the broth with the spices the meat released to form the jus.
Dip the slices in the hot jus for a few seconds.
Fill the rolls with the beef and a little jus; top with giardiniera or sweet peppers.
tips: Cool the meat in the refrigerator before slicing thinly and reheat the slices in the juices.
sources: Historia del Italian beef de Illinois

r-us-mw-detroit-pizza.summary: A rectangular pizza with a fluffy dough, a caramelized cheese edge, and stripes of tomato sauce on top.
r-us-mw-detroit-pizza.history: It originated in Detroit in the mid-20th century, when people began baking it in the blue steel industrial trays used in the automobile factories. The brick cheese spreads all the way to the edges and browns against the pan, forming a characteristic crispy crust. The sauce is laid in stripes over the cheese, in the 'red top' style.
ingredients: 350 g brick cheese, or mozzarella with Monterey Jack, spread to the edges
steps: Mix flour, yeast, salt, water and oil; knead, cover and let rise for 60 minutes until puffy.
Spread in an oiled rectangular pan and let rise another 30 minutes.
Cover with the cheese, bringing it right up to touch the pan walls.
Bake at 230°C for about 18 to 20 minutes until the edge cheese caramelizes.
Right out of the oven, draw stripes of tomato sauce over the surface and serve in squares.
tips: Spread cheese right to the pan walls to form the characteristic browned edge.
sources: Historia de la pizza de Detroit
Tradición de las charolas de acero de Míchigan

r-us-mw-coney-dog.summary: A hot dog on a bun topped with a beanless beef chili, yellow mustard, and chopped raw onion.
r-us-mw-coney-dog.history: Despite its name, which evokes New York's Coney Island, this dog has been a Detroit icon since the early 20th century, created by Greek and Macedonian immigrants who opened 'coney' shops. The spiced ground-meat sauce sets the city's rival houses apart and is served around the clock.
steps: Cook the ground beef, breaking it up very fine, with the chili powder, cumin, paprika, and tomato puree.
Simmer over low heat until you have a thick sauce with no large lumps.
Heat the hot dogs by steaming or on the griddle and warm the buns.
Place each hot dog in its bun and cover it with the meat sauce.
Finish with a line of mustard and plenty of chopped onion.
tips: Break up the beef as it cooks and check 71 °C before serving the sauce.
sources: Tradición de los coney islands de Detroit
Historia de la comida griega-americana de Míchigan

r-us-mw-cincinnati-chili.summary: A thin, spiced meat sauce with hints of cinnamon and chocolate, served over spaghetti and crowned with a mountain of cheese.
r-us-mw-cincinnati-chili.history: It was created in 1922 by the Kiradjieff brothers, Macedonian immigrants who opened the Empress restaurant next to a Cincinnati theater. They adapted Mediterranean and Middle Eastern spices into a meat sauce they served over spaghetti. You order it by 'ways': three-way has cheese, four-way adds onion, and five-way adds beans.
ingredients: 15 g dark chocolate or 1 tablespoon cocoa
300 g very finely grated cheddar cheese
steps: Boil the raw meat directly in the water, breaking it up so it stays very fine and doesn't brown.
Add the onion, chili powder, cinnamon, cumin, allspice, chocolate, and vinegar.
Simmer over low heat for about an hour and a half until it thickens and the flavors come together.
Serve a bed of hot spaghetti and cover it with the sauce.
Crown with a generous mountain of finely grated cheddar.
tips: Use already cooked spaghetti and keep it warm while finishing the meat sauce.
sources: Tradición del restaurante Empress de Ohio

r-us-mw-kc-burnt-ends.summary: Fatty smoked beef brisket points, caramelized twice and bathed in a sweet, thick barbecue sauce.
r-us-mw-kc-burnt-ends.history: They are the fatty tips of the smoked beef brisket, which became a delicacy in Kansas City. Their popularization is credited to Arthur Bryant's, where those trimmings were once given away to customers in line. A 1972 article by Calvin Trillin launched them to national fame. Today they are smoked separately, glazed, and caramelized again.
ingredients: Hickory or oak wood for smoking
steps: Rub the brisket with the mixture of salt, pepper, paprika, sugar, and garlic.
Smoke it over indirect heat at about 110°C until the internal temperature reaches 90°C.
Cut the point into cubes about three centimeters across.
Toss the cubes with the barbecue sauce and a little brown sugar.
Return the cubes to the smoker for another hour until they caramelize and turn sticky.
tips: The beef should be tender before cubing; the final hour sets the glaze.
sources: Historia de la barbacoa de Kansas City

r-us-mw-toasted-ravioli.summary: Breaded ravioli fried until golden, served with Parmesan cheese and marinara sauce for dipping.
r-us-mw-toasted-ravioli.history: They are associated with The Hill neighborhood of St. Louis, with its strong Italian heritage. According to local legend, around the 1950s a restaurant cook accidentally dropped some ravioli into hot oil instead of water, and the accident was such a hit that it became a specialty. They are served as a crispy appetizer.
ingredients: 24 meat or cheese ravioli, precooked and cold
steps: Coat each ravioli in flour, then egg, and finally breadcrumbs mixed with oregano.
Heat the oil to 180°C.
Fry the ravioli in batches until golden and crispy.
Drain them on paper towels and sprinkle with Parmesan right away.
Serve hot with marinara sauce for dipping.
tips: Use already cooked, cold and dry ravioli; meat-filled ravioli are not vegetarian.
sources: Tradición del barrio The Hill de San Luis
Historia de los toasted ravioli de Misuri

r-us-mw-gooey-butter-cake.summary: A flat, dense cake with a sweet dough base and a sticky top layer of butter and sugar, dusted with powdered sugar.
r-us-mw-gooey-butter-cake.history: This flat, gooey dessert was born in the German bakeries of south St. Louis around the 1930s or 1940s. The most repeated story says a baker mixed up the proportions of butter and flour, baked it anyway, and the sticky result delighted customers. Its exact inventor is still disputed.
steps: Mix flour, yeast, milk, base sugar and 60 g butter; knead and spread in a pan. Cover and let rise 1 hour.
Beat the remaining 120 g butter with topping sugar, eggs, syrup and vanilla.
Pour the topping over the dough without spreading it too much.
Bake at 175°C for about 40 minutes; the center should stay jiggly, not dry.
Let cool and dust generously with powdered sugar before cutting into squares.
tips: Use 60 g butter in the base and 120 g in the topping; cool before cutting.
sources: Historia del gooey butter cake de San Luis
Tradición de las panaderías alemanas de Misuri

r-us-mw-cheese-curds.summary: Chunks of fresh cheddar curds battered and fried, crispy outside and springy and squeaky inside.
r-us-mw-cheese-curds.history: Wisconsin, America's dairy heartland, made cheese curds (the fresh chunks that separate from the whey when making cheddar) an emblem. When very fresh, they squeak when you bite them. Battered and fried, they became a star of the state's fairs and regional breweries.
steps: Mix the flour, salt, and paprika with the egg and beer until you have a light batter.
Pat the cheese curds dry with paper towels.
Heat the oil to 190°C.
Dip the curds in the batter and fry them in short batches until golden.
Drain them and serve immediately, while they are still hot and stretchy.
tips: Fry small batches and serve immediately for a crisp coating and soft cheese.
sources: Historia de los cheese curds fritos

r-us-mw-sheboygan-brat.summary: A charcoal-grilled pork sausage served on a semmel roll with mustard, onion, and pickles, typical of Wisconsin's fry-outs.
r-us-mw-sheboygan-brat.history: German immigrants brought the bratwurst to Wisconsin, and Sheboygan proclaimed itself the sausage's world capital. The local custom is to grill it slowly over charcoal and sometimes soak it in beer and onion. It is served on a firm semmel-style roll, often doubled up, at outdoor gatherings called 'brat frys.'
steps: Heat the beer with the onion and butter in a wide pot.
Parboil the bratwurst in that beer over gentle heat without bursting the skin.
Grill, turning, until browned and the center reaches 71 °C; keep the beer bath hot.
Return them to the beer and onion bath to keep them juicy.
Serve each bratwurst on its roll with mustard, onion from the bath, and pickles.
tips: Poach gently and make sure fresh pork sausage reaches 71 °C before serving.
sources: Historia de la bratwurst en el Medio Oeste

r-us-mw-juicy-lucy.summary: A burger with the cheese sealed inside the patty, releasing a hot, molten cheese center when you bite in.
r-us-mw-juicy-lucy.history: It is a Minneapolis specialty claimed by two neighboring bars, Matt's Bar and the 5-8 Club, which both credit its invention to the mid-20th century. Instead of putting the cheese on top, it is enclosed between two layers of meat, so that cooking forms a lava-like core. You have to let it rest so you don't burn yourself.
ingredients: 700 g ground beef with some fat
steps: Divide the meat into eight thin patties and season them with salt and pepper.
Fold the cheese slices and place them in the center of four patties.
Cover with the other patties and seal the edges very well so the cheese doesn't escape.
Cook on a medium-hot griddle about 6-8 minutes per side, until the beef reaches 71 °C; insert the thermometer from the side and avoid measuring only the cheese.
Let rest a couple of minutes and serve on the bun with onion and pickles.
tips: Rest before the first bite because the cheese inside is very hot.

r-us-mw-tater-tot-hotdish.summary: A baked casserole of ground beef, vegetables, and cream, topped with a golden layer of tater tots.
r-us-mw-tater-tot-hotdish.history: The 'hotdish' is Minnesota's quintessential community casserole, popular at church suppers and family gatherings since the mid-20th century. It combines protein, vegetables, a canned cream soup as a base, and a crispy topping; the tater tot version is the most beloved and the cheapest to make for a crowd.
ingredients: 2 cups mixed vegetables (corn, peas, green beans)
steps: Brown the beef with the onion and season; drain the excess fat.
Mix the beef with the vegetables, cream of mushroom soup, and milk in a baking dish.
Arrange the tater tots to cover the whole surface in a single layer.
Bake at 190°C for about 40 minutes until the tots turn golden.
Sprinkle with the cheese and bake another 10 minutes until it melts.
tips: Arrange frozen potato pieces in a single layer and check 74 °C at the center of the casserole.
sources: Cocina comunitaria de las llanuras del norte

r-us-mw-runza.summary: A yeast bread stuffed with ground beef, cabbage, and onion, baked until golden, a heritage of the Volga Germans.
r-us-mw-runza.history: The Volga Germans, who emigrated from Russia to the plains of Nebraska, brought the bierock, a bread stuffed with meat and cabbage. Sally Everett adapted the family recipe, named it 'runza,' and in 1949 founded a restaurant chain in Lincoln that made the bun a Nebraska state emblem.
steps: Make the dough with flour, yeast, milk, sugar, butter and egg; cover and let rise about 60 minutes until doubled.
Brown the beef with the onion, add the cabbage, and cook until wilted; season and cool.
Roll out the dough and cut it into squares; place filling in the center of each.
Close the edges into sealed packets and place them seam-side down.
Bake at 190°C for about 20 to 25 minutes until golden.
tips: Cool the filling before enclosing it to avoid wetting or tearing the dough.
sources: Historia de la runza de Nebraska
Herencia culinaria de los alemanes del Volga

r-us-mw-pork-tenderloin-sandwich.summary: A pounded, breaded, and fried pork tenderloin fillet, so large it overhangs the bun by a wide margin.
r-us-mw-pork-tenderloin-sandwich.history: This pounded, breaded, and fried pork tenderloin sandwich is a Midwestern plains classic, strongly identified with Iowa and Indiana. It derives from the German schnitzel and is served on a small bun that the meat overhangs dramatically, accompanied only by mustard, pickles, and onion.
ingredients: 4 pork tenderloin fillets, about 120 g each
1 1/2 cups crushed saltine crackers or breadcrumbs
Mustard, pickles, and onion for serving
steps: Pound each fillet between plastic wrap until very thin and wide.
Season it and coat it in flour, egg, and cracker crumbs mixed with garlic powder.
Fry in oil at 180°C until golden and crispy on both sides.
Drain on paper towels.
Serve on the bun, letting the meat overhang, with mustard, pickles, and onion.
tips: Pound evenly, cook to 63 °C and rest 3 minutes before assembling.
sources: Tradición del pork tenderloin sandwich de Iowa

r-us-mw-chislic.summary: Cubes of red meat (lamb, beef, or bison) seasoned and fried or grilled, served on a toothpick with saltine crackers.
r-us-mw-chislic.history: Chislic is South Dakota's emblematic bite, so much so that it was declared the state's official 'nosh.' It is credited to immigrants of German-Russian origin who arrived from Central Asia in the 19th century. It consists of seasoned red-meat cubes, traditionally lamb or mutton and also plains beef or bison, served with saltine crackers and hot sauce.
ingredients: 700 g lamb, beef, or bison, cubed
steps: Marinate the meat cubes with garlic, Worcestershire sauce, garlic salt, and pepper for at least an hour.
Drain the meat well.
Fry it in hot oil or grill it in batches to the desired doneness, keeping it juicy inside.
Skewer the cubes on toothpicks and sprinkle with a little more garlic salt.
Serve hot with saltine crackers and hot sauce.
tips: Drain and dry the meat before frying; check 63 °C and rest 3 minutes.
sources: Tradición del chislic de Dakota del Sur
Herencia germano-rusa de las llanuras del norte

r-us-w-cioppino.summary: A seafood stew in a tomato and wine broth from San Francisco's Italian fishermen, with Dungeness crab, clams, mussels, and fish.
r-us-w-cioppino.history: It was born in the late 19th century among the Genoese fishermen of North Beach in San Francisco, who cooked what was left over from the day's catch in a big communal pot. Its name comes from 'ciuppin,' a Ligurian fisherman's soup, though local legend attributes it to the shout of 'chip in' with which fishermen asked others to contribute to the pot. The first printed recipe appeared in a San Francisco newspaper in the early 20th century.
ingredients: 1 cooked and cut-up Dungeness crab (or 500 g crab legs)
400 g firm white fish fillet, in chunks
1 bay leaf and a pinch of red pepper flakes
Chopped fresh parsley and olive oil
steps: Sauté the onion, fennel, and garlic in olive oil until tender.
Add the crushed tomatoes, white wine, fish stock, bay leaf, and red pepper flakes.
Let the broth simmer gently for about 20 minutes to concentrate the flavor.
First add the crab and clams; cover and cook 5 minutes.
Add the mussels, fish, and shrimp and cook until the shells open and the fish is opaque.
Discard any closed shells, adjust the salt, and serve with parsley and crusty bread for dipping.
tips: Add seafood in order of cooking time and discard shells that remain closed.
sources: Fisherman's Wharf, historia del cioppino de San Francisco
KQED: The Fishy Origins of Cioppino

r-us-w-mission-burrito.summary: A giant San Francisco-style burrito with rice, beans, meat, cheese, guacamole, and salsa, wrapped very tightly in a large flour tortilla.
r-us-w-mission-burrito.history: It emerged in the taquerias of San Francisco's Mission district around the 1960s and 1970s, within the Mexican-American community. Unlike the burrito of northern Mexico, the Mission style is huge, includes rice, and is wrapped in foil so you can eat it standing up. It became an icon of Californian fast food.
ingredients: 1 cup rice cooked with cilantro and lime
300 g carne asada, chicken, or carnitas, in pieces
Hot sauce and crema to taste
steps: Heat the tortilla on a comal until it is pliable.
Place the rice, beans, and hot meat in the center.
Add the cheese, guacamole, pico de gallo, and salsa.
Fold the sides in and roll tightly so it holds together firmly.
Wrap in foil, heat a few seconds on the comal to seal, and cut it in half to serve.
tips: Rice, beans and meat should be cooked and hot before assembling the burrito.
sources: Historia de las taquerías del barrio Mission, San Francisco

r-us-w-french-dip.summary: A roast beef sandwich on French bread served with a bowl of hot beef jus (au jus) for dipping.
r-us-w-french-dip.history: It was invented in Los Angeles around 1908-1918, though its exact origin is disputed between two historic restaurants: Philippe the Original and Cole's, both opened in 1908. Both claim the sandwich was born when a roll got dipped, by accident or at a customer's request, in the juice of the roast beef. It became popular as working-class food in the city's downtown.
ingredients: 800 g beef chuck or roasting cut
1 bay leaf and a few sprigs of thyme
steps: Season the meat with salt and pepper and sear it on all sides in a pot with hot oil.
Add the onion and garlic, the beef broth, the Worcestershire sauce, the bay leaf, and the thyme.
Cover and cook over low heat for about 90 minutes until the meat is very tender.
Remove the meat, let it rest, and slice it very thin; strain the cooking juice (au jus) and keep it hot.
Fill the rolls with the meat and serve each sandwich with a bowl of au jus on the side for dipping.
tips: Chuck can need more time than loin; cook until the selected cut is tender.
sources: Historia del French dip, Los Ángeles

r-us-w-green-chile-stew.summary: A comforting pork or beef stew with potato and plenty of roasted New Mexico green chile, a symbol of New Mexican cooking.
r-us-w-green-chile-stew.history: Green chile, especially the kind grown in the Hatch valley, is the heart of New Mexico's culinary identity. This stew combines the indigenous Pueblo tradition with the Hispanic tradition of the Southwest, using the autumn harvest chile that is roasted and frozen for the whole year. It is served on its own or with a tortilla, and the state question 'red or green?' sums up its importance.
ingredients: 6 to 8 New Mexico (or Anaheim) green chiles, roasted, peeled, and chopped
steps: Brown the pork cubes in hot oil and remove them.
In the same pot, sauté the onion and garlic until translucent; if using flour, sprinkle it in and cook a minute.
Return the meat, add the broth, cumin, and oregano, and let simmer gently 30 minutes.
Add the potatoes and the roasted green chile and cook until the potato is soft and the meat is tender.
Adjust the salt and serve hot with a flour tortilla.
tips: The wheat flour in this version means it is not gluten-free.
sources: New Mexico Department of Agriculture: Hatch green chile

r-us-w-nm-enchiladas.summary: New Mexico-style enchiladas served stacked in flat layers, bathed in red chile sauce and crowned with a fried egg.
r-us-w-nm-enchiladas.history: Unlike the rolled enchiladas of central Mexico, the New Mexican tradition makes them stacked: corn tortillas layered with cheese and onion, covered in a sauce of ground dried red chile. It is a distinctive dish of the state, a heritage of the Hispanic cooking of the Southwest, usually finished with a fried egg on top.
ingredients: 8 dried New Mexico red chiles, seeded
2 cups grated cheese (Monterey Jack or cheddar)
steps: Rehydrate the red chiles in hot water and blend them with garlic, cumin, oregano, salt, and broth until smooth.
Strain the sauce and cook it over low heat for about 10 minutes.
Pass each tortilla briefly through hot oil to soften it.
Assemble each portion by stacking sauce-dipped tortillas with cheese and onion between layers.
Cover with more sauce and cheese, and melt under the broiler.
Fry one egg per portion and place it on top before serving.
tips: Use vegetable stock to keep the dish vegetarian and serve the egg fully set.
sources: Recetario hispano del suroeste de Estados Unidos

r-us-w-sonoran-hot-dog.summary: A bacon-wrapped, griddled hot dog served on a bolillo roll with pinto beans, tomato, onion, jalapeño, and sauces.
r-us-w-sonoran-hot-dog.history: Originally from Sonora, Mexico (Hermosillo and Ciudad Obregón), it crossed the border and became an emblem of the street food of Tucson, Arizona, where by the late 2000s there were more than 200 stands selling it. Its hallmark is the bacon-wrapped sausage and the soft bolillo roll, loaded with toppings in the northwestern Mexican style.
steps: Wrap each sausage in a strip of bacon in a spiral.
Griddle them, turning, until the bacon is crispy and golden.
Lightly warm the bolillo rolls and open them from the top.
Place the sausage and cover it with pinto beans, tomato, and onion.
Finish with mayonnaise, mustard, and jalapeño sauce; serve with a blistered güero chile.
tips: Turn sausages to brown the bacon all around and use hot, already cooked beans.

r-us-w-navajo-taco.summary: Fluffy fry bread topped with beans, seasoned ground meat, lettuce, tomato, and cheese, served as an open taco.
r-us-w-navajo-taco.history: Fry bread emerged in the 19th century among Native American peoples, especially the Navajo, after the forced displacement known as the Long Walk, when the government handed out flour, lard, and sugar. From those ingredients this fried bread was born, and later the Navajo taco when toppings were added. Today it is a symbolic dish, at once a cultural pride and a reminder of a difficult history.
ingredients: Lettuce, tomato, onion, and grated cheese
steps: Mix the flour, baking powder, and salt; add the water and form a soft dough without over-kneading.
Let the dough rest about 20 minutes and divide it into balls; stretch each one into a disc.
Fry the discs in hot oil until they puff up and brown on both sides; drain.
Season and cook the ground meat; heat the beans.
On each fry bread place beans and meat, and crown with lettuce, tomato, onion, and cheese.
tips: Fry dough at about 175 °C and cook ground beef to 71 °C before assembling.
sources: Smithsonian: historia del fry bread navajo
Cocina de las naciones nativas del suroeste

r-us-w-rocky-mountain-trout.summary: A fresh whole trout dredged in flour and browned in butter, a classic of Colorado's rivers and campsites.
r-us-w-rocky-mountain-trout.history: Trout fishing in high-mountain streams is a living tradition in Colorado and the Rockies. The most classic way to prepare it is the simplest: floured and fried in butter beside the river, often wrapped in bacon. It is a campfire and table dish that celebrates the region's freshwater fish.
steps: Pat the trout dry and season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Dredge them in flour, coating them evenly.
Melt the butter in a skillet and brown the trout for about 4 to 5 minutes per side.
Add the lemon and, if you like, the slivered almonds to toast them at the end.
Serve immediately with parsley and the browned butter from the pan.
tips: Brown butter without burning it and check 63 °C in the fish.
sources: Cocina de las Montañas Rocosas de Colorado
Tradición de pesca de trucha del oeste de EE. UU.

r-us-w-denver-omelette.summary: An omelette filled with ham, bell pepper, onion, and cheese, a classic American breakfast born in the West.
r-us-w-denver-omelette.history: Also called a 'Western omelette,' it is associated with Colorado and the Old West. One theory holds that it derives from the 'Denver sandwich,' an egg filling with ham and onion that stagecoach and railroad cooks made with ingredients that kept well on the journey. Over time the filling came to be served as an omelette.
steps: Sauté the ham, bell pepper, and onion in a little butter until tender; set aside.
Beat the eggs with salt and pepper.
Melt butter in a skillet and pour in the egg; cook over medium heat, moving the edges.
When the egg is nearly set, place the filling and cheese on one half.
Fold the omelette over the filling and serve it when the cheese starts to melt.
tips: Cook eggs over medium-low heat and finish with a set center at 71 °C.

r-us-w-cedar-plank-salmon.summary: A Pacific salmon fillet grilled on a cedar plank that gives it a characteristic smoky aroma, a Northwest tradition.
r-us-w-cedar-plank-salmon.history: The indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast, in Washington and Oregon, cooked salmon fastened to cedar planks beside the fire. That ancestral technique lives on in the regional cuisine: the dampened wood infuses the fish with an unmistakable woodsy aroma. Salmon here is a central food, both cultural and economic.
ingredients: 600 g Pacific salmon fillet with skin
2 tablespoons maple syrup or brown sugar
steps: Soak the cedar plank in water for at least 1 hour so it doesn't burn.
Mix the maple syrup, mustard, and garlic and brush it on the salmon; season with salt and pepper.
Preheat the grill to medium heat and set the plank on it until it starts to crackle and smoke.
Place the salmon skin-side down on the plank, cover the grill, and cook 15 to 20 minutes.
Remove when the salmon flakes easily; serve with lemon and dill.
tips: Use only a cooking-safe plank, keep it away from direct flames and check 63 °C in the salmon.
sources: Tradición del salmón de los pueblos costeros de Washington

r-us-w-marionberry-pie.summary: A double-crust pie filled with marionberry, a hybrid blackberry created in Oregon with an intense, slightly tart flavor.
r-us-w-marionberry-pie.history: The marionberry is a hybrid blackberry developed at Oregon State University and released in 1956, named for Marion County, where it was trialed. Oregon is its main producer worldwide, and the berry became an emblem of the state. The pie made with it is a much-loved seasonal dessert in the region.
ingredients: 700 g fresh or frozen marionberries (or blackberries)
steps: Line a pan with one of the discs of dough.
Mix the berries with the sugar, cornstarch, lemon, and salt.
Pour the filling over the base and cover it with the second disc or with a lattice.
Seal the edges, cut a few vents for steam, and brush with egg.
Bake at 200°C for about 20 minutes, lower to 180°C, and bake until the filling bubbles and the crust turns golden.
Let cool completely so the filling sets before slicing.
tips: Wait at least 2 hours after baking for the filling to set before slicing.
sources: Oregon State University: origen de la marionberry

r-us-w-poke.summary: Cubes of fresh tuna marinated in soy sauce, sesame oil, onion, and seaweed, an iconic Hawaiian dish.
r-us-w-poke.history: Poke ('to cut into pieces' in Hawaiian) is an ancestral dish of Hawaii's native fishermen, who seasoned raw fish with sea salt, limu seaweed, and kukui nut. With the arrival of Japanese immigrants and others from Pacific islands, soy sauce and sesame oil were incorporated, giving rise to the modern version that is today a symbol of island cooking.
ingredients: 500 g tuna sourced for raw consumption from a supplier who controls fish-related hazards
1 tablespoon chopped wakame or limu seaweed
steps: Keep tuna refrigerated and ask the supplier about handling for raw consumption; freshness and a “sushi-grade” label do not guarantee the absence of pathogens. To avoid raw fish, cook to 63 °C and chill before mixing.
Mix the soy sauce with the sesame oil and the red pepper flakes.
Combine the tuna with the red onion, green onion, and seaweed.
Pour in the dressing and mix gently so the fish doesn't fall apart.
Refrigerate 10 minutes, sprinkle with sesame seeds, and serve on its own or over rice.
tips: Raw fish is unsuitable for pregnant people, young children, older adults and immunocompromised people; use the cooked alternative.

r-us-w-loco-moco.summary: A dish of white rice with a burger patty, fried egg, and gravy, comfort food created in Hilo, Hawaii.
r-us-w-loco-moco.history: It was born in 1949 at the Lincoln Grill in Hilo, on Hawaii's Big Island, when a group of teenagers from the Lincoln Wreckers asked for something cheap and filling: rice with a burger patty and gravy. They named it 'loco moco' after a friend's nickname. Later the characteristic fried egg was added, and the dish spread across all the islands.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon each soy sauce and Worcestershire sauce
steps: Form two patties, season and cook until the center reaches 71 °C; keep hot.
In the same skillet melt the butter, add the flour, and cook to make a roux.
Pour in the broth, soy sauce, and Worcestershire little by little, and cook until you have a thick gravy.
Fry eggs until white and yolk are firm; use pasteurized eggs if you prefer a less-set yolk.
Serve the rice in a bowl, place the patty, cover it with gravy, and crown with the fried egg.
tips: Keep rice and gravy hot while finishing the burgers and eggs.
sources: What's Cooking America: Loco Moco Recipe and History
HAWAIʻI Magazine: origen del loco moco en Hilo

r-us-w-spam-musubi.summary: A bite of pressed rice with a slice of glazed Spam, wrapped in a strip of nori seaweed, very popular as a snack in Hawaii.
r-us-w-spam-musubi.history: It is an example of Hawaii's culinary blending: it combines the rice and onigiri of Japanese immigration with Spam, the canned meat that became ubiquitous on the islands during and after World War II. It is sold in convenience stores and stands all over the islands as cheap, quick food.
ingredients: 3 sheets nori seaweed, cut into strips
steps: Cut the Spam into slices about 1 cm thick.
Make a glaze with the soy sauce, sugar, and mirin and cook the slices until they caramelize on both sides.
Place a strip of nori, set the mold on top, and press a layer of rice.
Put a slice of Spam on the rice and unmold.
Wrap the block with the nori strip, sealing with a little water, and serve.
tips: Lightly moisten the mold and gently press the rice; serve promptly or refrigerate.

r-us-w-funeral-potatoes.summary: A creamy grated-potato gratin with cheese, cream, and a crispy cornflake topping, a Utah classic.
r-us-w-funeral-potatoes.history: This gratin is associated with the Latter-day Saint community in Utah, where the Relief Societies used to bring it to gatherings after funerals, hence its name. It is a comfort and gathering dish, present at family dinners and parties throughout the state and the Intermountain region.
ingredients: 1 kg grated potato (fresh or frozen hash browns)
1 can condensed cream of chicken or mushroom soup
steps: Mix the grated potato with the condensed soup, sour cream, cheese, onion, and half of the butter.
Season with salt and pepper and spread the mixture in a greased baking dish.
Combine the crushed cornflakes with the rest of the butter.
Cover the gratin with that crispy mixture.
Bake at 180°C for about 45 to 50 minutes until it bubbles and the topping is golden.
tips: The chicken-soup version is not vegetarian; also check the mushroom soup’s ingredients.
sources: Tradición de las funeral potatoes en la región intermontañosa

r-us-w-alaskan-king-crab.summary: Alaskan king crab legs steamed and served with melted butter and lemon, a delicacy from the Bering Sea.
r-us-w-alaskan-king-crab.history: The king crab of the Bering Sea is one of the most prized products of Alaska's fishery, famous for its enormous legs of sweet meat. The fleet that catches it works in frigid, dangerous waters during very short seasons. It is prepared simply so as not to overshadow its flavor: steamed with butter.
ingredients: 1.5 kg Alaskan king crab legs (already cooked and frozen)
steps: Start with crab legs thawed in the refrigerator; thawing is not included in the listed times.
Set a steamer rack over boiling water and arrange the legs.
Steam covered for about 6 to 8 minutes, just to heat them through.
Melt the butter with the garlic to serve alongside.
Serve the legs with the melted butter, lemon wedges, and parsley.
tips: The legs are already cooked; heat according to the package without unnecessarily prolonged steaming.

r-us-s-shrimp-and-grits.summary: Shrimp sauteed with bacon and spices over creamy corn grits, the signature dish of the Lowcountry.
r-us-s-shrimp-and-grits.history: It was born on the low coast of South Carolina among the Gullah Geechee communities, descendants of enslaved Africans who farmed rice. At first it was eaten as a shrimping-season breakfast and was called 'shrimp and hominy,' served with ground corn instead of rice. Over time grits replaced the rice and the dish became an emblem of Charleston.
ingredients: Salt, pepper, and hot sauce to taste
steps: Bring the water or stock to a boil with salt, sprinkle in the grits, and cook over low heat, stirring, until creamy; stir in the cheese if using.
In a skillet, brown the bacon until it renders its fat and turns crisp; set aside.
In that same fat, saute the onion and garlic until softened.
Raise the heat, add the shrimp, and cook 2 to 3 minutes per side until they turn pink.
Finish with lemon juice, salt, pepper, and hot sauce; return the bacon to the pan.
Serve the shrimp over the hot grits and sprinkle with chives.
tips: Check the grits package because quick-cooking and stone-ground grits require different times.
sources: Two Hundred Years of Charleston Cooking (1930)
Levine Museum of the New South

r-us-s-nashville-hot-chicken.summary: Fried chicken drenched in a fiery cayenne-and-hot-oil paste, served over white bread with pickles.
r-us-s-nashville-hot-chicken.history: As the legend goes, it emerged in Nashville in the 1930s when Thornton Prince's girlfriend served him pepper-loaded chicken as revenge; he loved it, and the family perfected the recipe. Prince's Hot Chicken Shack, considered the birthplace of the dish and a pioneering Black-owned business, made it popular, and the city's festival brought it fame in the 2000s.
ingredients: 1/2 cup of the hot frying oil or lard
Slices of white bread and pickles to serve
steps: Marinate the chicken in the buttermilk with salt for at least 2 hours or overnight.
Beat the egg with a little buttermilk; dredge each piece in seasoned flour, then the wet mixture, and again in flour.
Fry in oil at 165 °C until golden and cooked through; drain.
Mix the cayenne, paprika, sugar, and salt with the 1/2 cup of hot frying oil to form a paste.
Brush the chicken generously with the fiery paste.
Serve over white bread with pickles on top.
tips: Check 74 °C near but not touching the bone; if the outside browns too fast, finish in an oven at 180 °C.

r-us-s-kentucky-hot-brown.summary: An open-faced, broiled turkey sandwich with Mornay sauce, bacon, and tomato, baked until bubbling.
r-us-s-kentucky-hot-brown.history: It was created by chef Fred K. Schmidt in 1926 at the Brown Hotel in Louisville, Kentucky. Each night the hotel hosted hundreds of diners after the dance, and they had grown tired of the traditional ham-and-egg plates; Schmidt came up with this open-faced turkey sandwich with Mornay sauce, which soon became the house favorite. It is a variation on Welsh rarebit.
ingredients: 4 thick slices of sandwich bread (Texas toast style)
1/2 cup grated Parmesan or Pecorino cheese
Salt, pepper, and nutmeg to taste
steps: Fry the bacon until crisp and set aside.
Make the Mornay sauce: melt the butter, add the flour, and cook for a minute; gradually whisk in the milk until thickened.
Off the heat, stir in the cheese and season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
Toast the bread and place it in individual baking dishes; top with the turkey.
Ladle the Mornay sauce over it, covering the edges of the bread well.
Broil in the oven until bubbling and golden; crown with the bacon and tomato.
tips: Keep the sauce fluid enough to coat the turkey; add hot milk if it thickens before broiling.

r-us-s-cuban-sandwich.summary: A pressed Cuban-bread sandwich with roast pork, ham, salami, Swiss cheese, mustard, and pickles.
r-us-s-cuban-sandwich.history: It took shape in Ybor City, in south Tampa, Florida, in the early 20th century among Cuban, Spanish, and Italian immigrants who worked in the cigar factories. The Tampa press already mentioned it in 1906; it is said that at the Columbia Restaurant, Genoa salami was added around 1905 to please the Italians, a feature that distinguishes the Tampa cubano from the Miami one.
ingredients: 1 loaf Cuban bread or soft baguette (2 servings)
steps: Split the bread open and spread the inside with mustard.
Layer on the ham, roast pork, salami, Swiss cheese, and pickles.
Close the sandwich and spread butter on the outside.
Press it on a griddle or in a skillet with a weight on top over medium heat.
Press and toast on both sides until the bread is crisp and the cheese melts.
Cut on the diagonal and serve hot.
tips: Use already cooked meats and medium heat so the cheese melts before the bread burns.

r-us-s-key-lime-pie.summary: A pie with a creamy, tart Key lime filling made with condensed milk, on a graham cracker crust.
r-us-s-key-lime-pie.history: It is the signature dessert of the Florida Keys, where the small, aromatic Key lime grows. It became popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when canned condensed milk made it possible to prepare the filling without fresh refrigeration, something valuable on the islands before the railroad arrived.
steps: Mix the crackers with the sugar and butter; press into a pan to form the crust.
Bake the crust at 175 °C for about 8 minutes and let cool.
Beat the yolks with the zest until pale.
Stir in the condensed milk and then the lime juice until you have a smooth filling.
Pour over the crust and bake 12 to 15 minutes until set but not browned.
Chill completely in the refrigerator and serve with whipped cream.
tips: Bake the base for 8 minutes, then the filling for 12-15; the 3-hour chilling period is included in the total.

r-us-s-carolina-pulled-pork.summary: Slow-cooked, pulled pork dressed with a tangy, spicy vinegar sauce, the hallmark of North Carolina barbecue.
r-us-s-carolina-pulled-pork.history: Whole-hog barbecue is one of the oldest culinary traditions in North Carolina, with colonial and African American roots. The eastern style of the state uses the whole hog dressed only with vinegar and chili flakes, no tomato, unlike the western style, which uses the shoulder and a sauce with a touch of tomato.
steps: Rub the shoulder with the salt, pepper, paprika, and sugar.
Cook over very low heat (smoker or oven at 120 °C) for several hours until the meat falls apart.
Make the sauce by mixing the vinegar, chili flakes, hot sauce, and a pinch of salt.
Let the meat rest, then pull it apart with two forks.
Dress it with the vinegar sauce to taste and mix well.
Serve on its own or on soft buns, with extra sauce on the side.
tips: Pork shoulder is ready when easily shredded, often near 93 °C internally; size can extend the cooking time.

r-us-s-chili-con-carne.summary: A thick beef stew with dried chiles and cumin, with no beans in its classic Texas version.
r-us-s-chili-con-carne.history: It is associated with South Texas and especially San Antonio, where in the late 19th century the 'chili queens' sold the stew in the plazas. The Tex-Mex recipe blends the Mexican tradition of chiles with beef from Texas cattle; authentic 'chili con carne' does without beans and large amounts of tomato.
ingredients: 1 kg beef, cubed or coarsely ground
steps: Lightly toast the chiles, rehydrate them in hot water, and blend with the garlic and a little of the water.
Sear the beef in the lard until browned.
Add the onion and cook until softened.
Stir in the chile puree, cumin, and oregano; cook for a couple of minutes.
Pour in the stock, cover, and simmer over low heat about 2 hours until the beef is very tender and the sauce thick.
Adjust the salt and serve hot.
tips: Toast chiles without burning and adjust thickness with stock before serving.
sources: Historia de las chili queens de San Antonio

r-us-s-breakfast-tacos.summary: Flour tortilla tacos filled with egg plus bacon, potato, or beans, the signature breakfast of Texas.
r-us-s-breakfast-tacos.history: They are an everyday part of Tex-Mex breakfast, deeply rooted in San Antonio and Austin, where taquerias serve them from dawn. They combine the flour tortilla of northern Mexico and South Texas with fillings such as egg, bacon, potato, chorizo, or beans, a reflection of the region's Mexican American culture.
ingredients: Red or green salsa to taste
steps: Brown the bacon in a skillet until crisp.
In the same fat, saute the potato until lightly golden.
Lower the heat, pour in the beaten eggs with salt, and scramble until set.
Warm the flour tortillas on a griddle.
Fill each tortilla with the egg, bacon, potato, and cheese.
Serve right away with salsa and, if you like, refried beans.
tips: Start with cooked potatoes and beans and fully set the eggs over gentle heat.
sources: Tradición del desayuno de San Antonio y Austin

r-us-s-shrimp-poboy.summary: A crusty New Orleans baguette filled with breaded, fried shrimp, with lettuce, tomato, and mayonnaise.
r-us-s-shrimp-poboy.history: It was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, in 1929, when the Martin brothers, former streetcar conductors, offered free sandwiches to striking workers and called them 'poor boys.' It is served on local French bread with a thin crust and airy crumb; 'dressed' versions come with lettuce, tomato, pickles, and mayonnaise.
steps: Season the shrimp with salt, pepper, and a little hot sauce.
Dip them in the egg-and-milk mixture and then in the cornmeal combined with the flour.
Fry in hot oil until golden and crisp; drain.
Split the baguette open and spread mayonnaise inside.
Add lettuce, tomato, and the fried shrimp.
Close the sandwich and serve right away.
tips: Fry shrimp at 175-180 °C until the flesh is opaque and the coating crisp.

r-us-s-southern-fried-chicken.summary: Chicken pieces marinated in buttermilk, breaded, and fried to a golden, crispy crust.
r-us-s-southern-fried-chicken.history: Fried chicken is one of the pillars of Southern cooking and soul food. It combines the frying techniques of Scottish immigrants with the seasoning and spices brought by enslaved African Americans in the Deep South. It became a Sunday and celebration dish in states like Georgia and across the region.
steps: Marinate the chicken in the buttermilk with salt for at least 4 hours or overnight.
Mix the flour with the paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, salt, and pepper.
Drain the chicken and dredge it in the seasoned flour, pressing well.
Heat the oil to 165 °C.
Fry the pieces in batches until golden and cooked through.
Drain on a rack and let rest a few minutes before serving.
tips: Check 74 °C in the thickest piece and drain on a rack to retain the crust.

r-us-s-country-ham.summary: Salt-cured, smoked pork ham, pan-fried in golden slices and served with red-eye gravy.
r-us-s-country-ham.history: Salt-curing ham is a colonial tradition of Virginia; the town of Smithfield gave it international fame with its aged ham. This country ham, very salty and intensely flavored, is eaten in thin slices, often with red-eye gravy made from the pan drippings and coffee, a staple of the rural Southern breakfast.
ingredients: 4 slices commercial country ham, already cooked and ready to eat
1/2 cup black coffee (for the red-eye gravy)
Biscuits or bread on the side
steps: Heat the butter or fat in a skillet over medium heat.
Brown the ham slices for a couple of minutes per side without drying them out; remove them.
Pour the coffee into the hot skillet to deglaze and scrape up the golden drippings.
Let it reduce for a minute to form the red-eye gravy.
Serve the ham with the gravy on top and biscuits on the side.
tips: This recipe starts with cooked ham; if you buy uncooked cured ham, follow its cooking instructions before making the sauce.
sources: Tradición del jamón de Smithfield, Virginia
Cocina rural del sur de EE. UU.

r-us-s-collard-greens.summary: Collard leaves slow-cooked with smoked meat and their spiced broth (potlikker), a soul food classic.
r-us-s-collard-greens.history: Collard greens are a centerpiece of African American soul food in the Deep South, including Mississippi. They descend from African techniques of long-cooking leafy greens; they are stewed with smoked pork, and the resulting broth, the 'potlikker,' is prized as much as the greens and sipped with cornbread.
ingredients: 2 large bunches of collard greens, stemmed and cut into strips
1 smoked ham bone or 150 g bacon
steps: Saute the bacon or brown the ham hock in a large pot.
Add the onion and garlic and cook until softened.
Stir in the stock and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the collard leaves in batches and let them wilt down.
Cover and cook over low heat about an hour and a half until very tender.
Season with vinegar, salt, pepper, and chili flakes; serve with its potlikker.
tips: Wash leaves in several changes of water to remove sand and serve with some cooking broth.
sources: Soul food del sur de EE. UU.

r-us-s-cornbread.summary: Cornmeal bread baked in a cast-iron skillet, with a crisp crust and tender crumb, only lightly sweet.
r-us-s-cornbread.history: Cornbread is a staple of Appalachia and all of Southern cooking, an heir to Indigenous use of corn. The Southern and mountain version, like that of West Virginia, is barely sweet and is baked in a preheated cast-iron skillet with fat to achieve its signature crust; it accompanies stews, beans, and greens.
steps: Preheat the oven to 220 °C and put a cast-iron skillet with the fat inside to heat.
Mix the cornmeal with the salt and baking soda.
Separately, beat the egg with the buttermilk.
Combine the wet ingredients with the dry ones without overmixing.
Pour the batter into the hot greased skillet, which should sizzle.
Bake about 25 minutes until golden; turn out and serve hot.
tips: The preheated skillet forms a crust; handle it with dry oven mitts when pouring batter.
sources: Tradición sureña del pan de maíz

r-us-s-banana-pudding.summary: A layered dessert of vanilla custard, banana, and vanilla wafers, topped with meringue or whipped cream.
r-us-s-banana-pudding.history: Banana pudding is a much-loved dessert throughout the American South, including Alabama, made popular in the early 20th century when bananas became affordable and cookie brands spread the recipe. It alternates layers of custard, banana slices, and vanilla wafers that soften until creamy.
steps: Heat the milk without letting it boil.
Beat the yolks with the sugar and cornstarch; add some of the hot milk to temper.
Return everything to the pot and cook, stirring, until it thickens into a custard; stir in the vanilla.
In a baking dish, alternate layers of wafers, banana slices, and custard.
Repeat the layers and finish with custard.
Let cool slightly, cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours. Add whipped cream before serving.
tips: Cover the custard directly against its surface while chilling to prevent a skin forming.
sources: Postres tradicionales del sur de EE. UU.

r-us-s-chicken-fried-steak.summary: A breaded, fried steak cooked like chicken, served with white pepper gravy.
r-us-s-chicken-fried-steak.history: This breaded steak is associated with the South and Southwest of the U.S., especially Texas and Oklahoma. Its origin is credited to German and Austrian immigrants who arrived in Texas in the mid-19th century and adapted the Wiener schnitzel, using cheaper, tougher cuts of beef, breaded and fried with the fried-chicken technique.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons of the flour and frying drippings
Salt and plenty of black pepper
steps: Season the steaks with salt and pepper.
Dredge them in flour, then in the egg-and-milk mixture, and again in flour.
Fry them in hot oil until golden and crisp; set aside.
Pour off nearly all the oil, leaving the drippings and a few tablespoons of fat.
Add flour and cook for a minute; whisk in the milk until the gravy thickens.
Season with plenty of pepper and serve the white gravy over the steaks.
tips: Reserve 3 tablespoons clean flour for the sauce and cook the roux before adding the 2 cups milk.

r-us-s-fried-pickles.summary: Pickle slices battered and fried until crisp, served with a creamy dipping sauce.
r-us-s-fried-pickles.history: Fried pickles were invented in 1963 at the Duchess Drive-In near Atkins, Arkansas, when Bernell 'Fatman' Austin, inspired by the neighboring pickle plant, breaded and fried pickle slices. The appetizer spread across the South and today is a classic of bars and fairs.
ingredients: Ranch or remoulade sauce to serve
steps: Pat the pickles dry with paper towels so the batter sticks.
Mix the flour with the cornmeal, paprika, and salt.
Dip the pickles in the egg-and-buttermilk mixture and then in the flour.
Fry them in hot oil until they float and turn golden.
Drain them on paper towels.
Serve them hot with ranch or remoulade sauce.
tips: Dry pickle slices before coating so the crust adheres.
sources: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Fried Dill Pickles
THV11: History of deep fried pickles

r-us-ne-new-england-clam-chowder.summary: A creamy clam soup with potato, onion, and pork belly, thick and pale, the emblem of the New England coast.
r-us-ne-new-england-clam-chowder.history: The creamy version (with milk or cream) is the one most associated with Boston and all of New England, in contrast to the Manhattan version made with tomato. It was born among fishermen and coastal communities who made use of the quahog clams abundant in the area; it became popular in the 19th century and today is served in a bowl or a bread bowl. In Boston it is such an ingrained tradition that the city once passed a law banning the addition of tomato.
ingredients: 1 kg fresh clams (or 400 g canned chopped clams with their juice)
120 g pork belly or bacon, diced
Salt, pepper, and oyster crackers to serve
steps: If using fresh clams, steam them until they open; reserve the strained liquid and chop the meat.
In a pot, brown the pork belly; pour off some of the fat and add the butter.
Saute the onion and celery until translucent; sprinkle in the flour and cook for a minute.
Gradually pour in the clam stock, stirring, add the potato and bay leaf, and cook until the potato is tender.
Lower the heat, stir in the milk and cream, and warm without letting it boil.
Add the chopped clams, adjust the salt and pepper, and serve with oyster crackers.
tips: Discard unopened clams and strain their liquid through a fine filter to remove sand.
sources: Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia y prensa culinaria de Boston

r-us-ne-lobster-roll.summary: A butter-toasted bun filled with cold lobster meat bound with mayonnaise, celery, and lemon, an icon of the Maine summer.
r-us-ne-lobster-roll.history: Although the origin of the lobster sandwich is usually placed in Milford, Connecticut, in the 1920s, the Maine style (cold lobster with mayonnaise) became the emblem of the Maine coast, where American lobster is the most important catch. It is sold at shacks and stands by the sea and contrasts with the Connecticut style, which uses warm lobster bathed in butter.
ingredients: 450 g cooked lobster meat, cut into chunks
4 top-split hot dog buns (New England split-top)
steps: Mix the lobster with the mayonnaise, celery, lemon juice, and chives; season and refrigerate.
Spread butter on the sides of the buns.
Toast the buns in a skillet over medium heat until golden on the outside.
Fill each bun generously with the cold lobster mixture.
Serve right away, with extra lemon to taste.
tips: Use already cooked, cold lobster and fill freshly toasted buns just before eating.
sources: Comparativas Maine vs. Connecticut de prensa gastronómica

r-us-ne-maryland-crab-cakes.summary: Blue crab cakes with very little filler, seasoned with Old Bay and browned until crisp on the outside.
r-us-ne-maryland-crab-cakes.history: The blue crab of Chesapeake Bay is a symbol of Maryland cooking. Traditional crab cakes pride themselves on packing in as much crab meat as possible and just enough binder, brightened with Old Bay seasoning, a spice blend born in Baltimore. They are served fried or baked, on their own or in a sandwich.
steps: Beat the egg with the mayonnaise, mustard, Worcestershire sauce, Old Bay, and lemon juice.
Stir in the crushed crackers and parsley.
Fold in the crab meat carefully, mixing without breaking up the lumps.
Form into cakes and refrigerate them 20 minutes so they firm up.
Brown them in butter over medium heat about 4 minutes per side, or bake them, until golden.
Serve with lemon wedges and tartar sauce.
tips: Keep the crab pieces intact and chill the cakes before browning so they hold their shape.
sources: Cocina de la bahía de Chesapeake
Tradición de Baltimore y el condimento Old Bay

r-us-ne-philly-cheesesteak.summary: A sandwich of thinly sliced griddled beef with melted cheese on a long roll, the signature sandwich of Philadelphia.
r-us-ne-philly-cheesesteak.history: It was created around 1930 by brothers Pat and Harry Olivieri, owners of a hot dog stand in South Philadelphia, when they grilled beef with onion instead of sausages. The cheese came later; with the arrival of Cheez Whiz in the 1950s it became one of the classic options, along with provolone and American. Pat's King of Steaks is still on the corner of 9th and Wharton.
ingredients: 400 g beef round or rib eye, very thinly sliced
Cheez Whiz, provolone, or sliced American cheese
steps: Heat the griddle or skillet with a little oil and saute the onion (and the mushrooms or pepper if using) until browned.
Add the sliced beef and saute it while chopping it up with the spatula, seasoning with salt and pepper.
Gather the beef and onion together and place the cheese on top so it melts.
Split the roll open and use it to scoop up the mixture with the melted cheese.
Serve right away.
tips: Chill the meat before slicing thinly and cook on a wide, hot surface.
sources: Historia de Pat's King of Steaks

r-us-ne-ny-pizza-slice.summary: A large, thin, foldable slice of crisp dough, tomato sauce, and mozzarella, folded in half to eat standing up.
r-us-ne-ny-pizza-slice.history: Neapolitan pizza arrived with Italian immigration; the first licensed pizzeria in the United States, Lombardi's, opened in Manhattan in 1905. Over time the New York style emerged: thin, elastic dough baked in a gas oven, sold by the slice at 'slice shops.' Folding the slice in half to eat it while walking is part of the ritual.
ingredients: Dried oregano and basil to taste
steps: Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the water; mix with the flour, salt, and oil until you have a smooth dough.
Let it ferment, covered, at least 1 hour until doubled in volume (better overnight in the refrigerator).
Stretch the dough very thin on a hot tray or stone.
Season the crushed tomatoes with salt and oregano and spread them, leaving a border free.
Distribute the mozzarella and bake at the oven's maximum temperature until the edge is golden and crisp.
Cut into large slices, sprinkle with basil, and serve.
tips: The minimum first rise is included in preparation; an overnight rise adds to the total time.
sources: Historia de Lombardi's y la pizza en Nueva York
Tradición de las slice shops neoyorquinas

r-us-ne-bagel-lox.summary: A split bagel spread with cream cheese, cured salmon (lox), red onion, tomato, and capers, a New York brunch classic.
