r-us-ne-bagel-lox.history: The bagel arrived with Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe and became an essential part of New York's food culture. The combination with cream cheese and lox (salted, not smoked, in its original form) became popular in the city's 'appetizing stores' and today is the weekend breakfast par excellence.
steps: Cut the bagels in half and toast them lightly.
Spread a generous layer of cream cheese on each half.
Lay the salmon slices on top.
Add the red onion, tomato, and capers.
Finish with dill and pepper and serve open-faced.
tips: Keep salmon and cream cheese refrigerated until assembling the bagel.
sources: Cultura del delicatessen judío de Nueva York

r-us-ne-pastrami-on-rye.summary: A tall sandwich of cured, smoked beef pastrami, hand-cut, served on rye bread with mustard.
r-us-ne-pastrami-on-rye.history: Beef pastrami, an inheritance of Eastern European Jewish cooking (related to Romanian pastrama), became an emblem of New York's delicatessens. Katz's Delicatessen, on the Lower East Side since 1888, is its temple. The meat is cured, seasoned with spices, smoked, and steamed before being sliced.
steps: Warm the pastrami with steam for a few minutes so it is juicy and warm.
Spread mustard on the slices of rye bread.
Pile a generous portion of pastrami on the bread.
Close the sandwich and cut it in half.
Serve with pickles on the side.
tips: Warm pastrami with gentle steam so it does not dry out before assembling.

r-us-ne-buffalo-wings.summary: Fried chicken wings drenched in a hot sauce with butter, served with celery and blue cheese dressing.
r-us-ne-buffalo-wings.history: They were created in 1964 at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, New York, where Teressa Bellissimo fried wings and coated them in hot sauce, serving them with celery and blue cheese because that was what she had on hand. From that improvised snack came one of the most widespread appetizers in the United States.
ingredients: Blue cheese dressing on the side
steps: Pat the wings dry and fry them in hot oil until golden and crisp.
Melt the butter and mix it with the hot sauce (and the vinegar) until combined.
Drain the wings and toss them in a bowl with the sauce to coat.
Serve right away with celery and blue cheese dressing.
tips: Fry in batches and check 74 °C in the wings before coating with sauce.
sources: Historia del Anchor Bar de Búfalo

r-us-ne-boston-baked-beans.summary: Beans slow-baked with molasses and salt pork, sweet and thick, enough to earn Boston the nickname 'Beantown.'
r-us-ne-boston-baked-beans.history: This dish of beans slow-cooked with molasses and salt pork has colonial roots in New England, tied to the molasses and rum trade and the Puritan custom of cooking them on Saturday so as not to work on Sunday. They became so popular that Boston earned the nickname 'Beantown.'
ingredients: 150 g salt pork or bacon, cut into pieces
steps: Drain the soaked beans and cook them 30 minutes in water until they start to soften; reserve the liquid.
Place the onion at the bottom of a bean pot or casserole and add the beans with the salt pork.
Mix the molasses, sugar, mustard, and salt with cooking liquid and pour it in to cover.
Bake, covered, at 150 °C for several hours, adding hot water as they dry out.
Uncover for the last hour so they thicken and brown, then serve.
tips: Keep beans covered with liquid during covered cooking and uncover only when tender.

r-us-ne-whoopie-pie.summary: Two soft chocolate cakes embracing a creamy filling of buttercream or marshmallow.
r-us-ne-whoopie-pie.history: Its origin is disputed among Maine, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts. Pennsylvania claims it from the cooking of the Pennsylvania Dutch (Amish), who reportedly made it with leftover cake batter; Maine declared it its official treat in 2011 and associates it with Labadie's Bakery in Lewiston around 1925. The marshmallow-cream recipe spread through the Marshmallow Fluff brand.
ingredients: For the filling: 200 g marshmallow fluff
For the filling: 100 g butter and 1 cup powdered sugar
steps: Beat the melted butter with the sugar, egg, and vanilla.
Alternate the flour sifted with cocoa and baking soda with the milk until you have a dense batter.
Place rounded portions on a tray and bake at 180 °C for about 10-12 minutes; let cool.
For the filling, beat the butter with the powdered sugar and marshmallow fluff until fluffy.
Join the cakes in pairs with a generous layer of filling.
tips: Cool the cakes completely before filling so the cream does not melt.
sources: Debate sobre el origen del whoopie pie (Maine, Pensilvania, Massachusetts)
Declaración de Maine como golosina oficial (2011)

r-us-ne-clam-cakes.summary: Fried balls of batter with chopped clams, crisp outside and fluffy inside, classics of the coastal shacks.
r-us-ne-clam-cakes.history: Clam cakes, or clam fritters, are a fixture of Rhode Island's seafood stands, especially by Narragansett Bay. They are served by the dozen and usually accompanied by a clear Rhode Island-style clam broth. They are beach and summer food par excellence in the smallest state in the country.
ingredients: 1 cup chopped clams (fresh or canned), drained
steps: Mix the flour, baking powder, salt, and pepper.
Beat the egg with the milk or clam juice and stir it into the dry ingredients.
Add the chopped clams to form a thick batter.
Heat plenty of oil to 180 °C.
Drop in spoonfuls of batter and fry until golden and cooked through.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot.
tips: Make small portions so the centers cook before the outsides brown too much.
sources: Tradición de los clam shacks de Rhode Island
Cocina de la bahía de Narragansett

r-us-ne-coffee-milk.summary: A cold milk drink sweetened with coffee syrup, similar to chocolate milk but coffee-flavored, the official drink of Rhode Island.
r-us-ne-coffee-milk.history: Coffee milk became popular in Rhode Island starting in the 1920s, possibly among the Italian community of Providence. It is made with coffee syrup (local brands like Autocrat) and became such a beloved state symbol that in 1993 it was declared the official drink of Rhode Island, over its rival, frozen lemonade.
steps: Pour the cold milk into a glass.
Add the coffee syrup.
Stir well until the color and flavor are blended in.
Serve over ice if you like.
tips: Mix the syrup with a little milk first, then add the rest to blend evenly.
sources: Declaración de coffee milk como bebida oficial de Rhode Island (1993)
State Symbols USA y prensa local

r-us-ne-new-haven-clam-apizza.summary: A pizza with no tomato sauce, thin and charred, topped with fresh clams, garlic, oregano, oil, and grated cheese.
r-us-ne-new-haven-clam-apizza.history: New Haven 'apizza,' from Connecticut, is a tradition of Italian immigrants baked in a coal oven. The white clam version became popular at Frank Pepe Pizzeria Napoletana around the 1960s, when freshly shucked clams were placed over a white base with garlic and oil. It is one of the most celebrated pizzas in the country.
ingredients: 24 fresh littleneck clams, shucked and chopped (with their juice)
steps: Stretch the dough very thin on a floured surface or peel.
Brush the base with olive oil and scatter the minced garlic.
Distribute the chopped clams with a little of their juice.
Sprinkle the Pecorino and oregano and drizzle with more oil.
Bake at maximum temperature (ideally on a stone) until the edge browns and chars slightly.
Serve straight from the oven with chili flakes if you like.
tips: Preheat the stone or tray thoroughly and cook until the clams are opaque, not just until the rim browns.
sources: Historia de Frank Pepe Pizzeria Napoletana
Tradición de la apizza de New Haven

r-us-ne-pork-roll-egg-cheese.dishName: Pork roll, egg and cheese (Taylor ham)
r-us-ne-pork-roll-egg-cheese.summary: A breakfast sandwich with fried pork roll, egg, and American cheese on a roll, the classic New Jersey morning fare.
r-us-ne-pork-roll-egg-cheese.history: Pork roll, known as 'Taylor ham' in North Jersey, is a cured pork product created in the 19th century by John Taylor in Trenton. The pork roll, egg, and cheese sandwich is the state's quintessential street breakfast, the subject of a fond regional debate over what to call it.
steps: Make a small cut at the edge of each pork roll slice so it does not curl, and fry until browned on both sides.
In the same skillet, cook the egg to your liking and season with salt and pepper.
Place the cheese on the hot pork roll so it melts.
Toast the roll lightly.
Assemble the sandwich with the pork roll, cheese, and egg, and add ketchup if you like.
tips: Cut shallow radial slits in the pork roll to keep it flat in the pan.
sources: Historia del pork roll / Taylor ham de Trenton
Tradición del desayuno de Nueva Jersey

r-us-ne-soft-pretzel.summary: A large, soft baked pretzel with a golden crust and coarse salt, sold on the streets of Philadelphia with mustard.
r-us-ne-soft-pretzel.history: The pretzel came to Pennsylvania with German immigrants (Pennsylvania Dutch), and Philadelphia adopted it as street food. The city's soft pretzel usually has an elongated shape and is sold on street corners to eat with yellow mustard. The region still has pretzel bakeries and factories with more than a century of history.
ingredients: 1/2 cup baking soda (for the bath water)
steps: Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water; mix with the flour and salt and knead until you have a smooth dough.
Let it rest, covered, until doubled in volume.
Divide the dough, form long ropes, and give them the classic pretzel shape.
Dip each pretzel for a few seconds in boiling water with the baking soda.
Place them on the tray, sprinkle with coarse salt, and bake at 220 °C until deeply golden.
Serve warm with yellow mustard.
tips: Use 2 liters water for the baking-soda bath and dip each piece about 30 seconds.

r-us-ne-sugar-on-snow.dishName: Sugar on snow (maple syrup on snow)
r-us-ne-sugar-on-snow.summary: A treat of hot maple syrup poured over snow, where it sets into sticky strands eaten like candy.
r-us-ne-sugar-on-snow.history: Vermont is the largest producer of maple syrup in the United States. During the harvest season (sugaring season, in late winter), it is tradition to boil the syrup and pour it over clean snow so it solidifies into a chewy treat. It is typically served with pickles and doughnuts to cut the sweetness.
ingredients: 500 g shaved ice made from drinking water
Pickles and doughnuts on the side
steps: Prepare trays of shaved drinking-water ice and keep frozen until needed.
Heat the maple syrup over medium heat until it reaches about 112-115 °C (soft-ball/thread stage).
Pour strands of hot syrup over the snow, where it will set instantly.
Roll up the sticky strands with a fork or stick and eat them like candy.
Serve with pickles and doughnuts to balance the sweetness.
tips: Drizzle thin strands of syrup over drinking-water ice; hot caramel can cause burns.
sources: Tradición del sugaring season de Vermont
Cultura del jarabe de arce de Nueva Inglaterra

r-it-pasta-carbonara.summary: Roman pasta with guanciale, pecorino, egg and pepper, made creamy by emulsification without added cream.
r-it-pasta-carbonara.history: Carbonara is associated with Rome and Lazio. Its modern history has several explanations and no single undisputed attribution.
steps: Cook pasta in lightly salted water and reserve 300 ml of cooking water.
Brown the guanciale over medium-low heat until crisp and its fat has rendered.
Beat the pasteurized eggs and yolks with pecorino and pepper in a bowl.
Add pasta to the skillet and turn off the heat. Wait briefly, add the egg mixture and stir vigorously.
Add pasta water gradually until creamy and smooth. Serve immediately.
tips: Finely grate the cheese and turn off the heat before adding eggs.

r-it-pizza-napoletana.summary: Tomato, buffalo mozzarella and basil pizza made with already fermented dough.
r-it-pizza-napoletana.history: Naples is central to this pizza tradition. This home version adapts cooking temperature and time to the available oven.
steps: Preheat an oven with a stone or heavy tray at 250-275 °C for 30 minutes.
Divide dough in two and stretch by hand, keeping a thicker rim.
Add tomato, salt and drained mozzarella. Bake each pizza 8-12 minutes until the base is cooked and the rim browned.
Add basil and oil. In a pizza oven at 450 °C, cook about 60-90 seconds, watching and turning the pizza.
tips: Fermented dough is a prepared ingredient; making it from scratch adds fermentation time.

r-it-risotto-milanese.summary: Creamy saffron rice with bone marrow, butter and Parmesan.
r-it-risotto-milanese.history: Saffron risotto is a Milan specialty. Stories of its beginnings are part of local tradition; this is a home version.
steps: Soak saffron in a ladle of hot stock. Gently sauté the onion in 25 g butter and the marrow.
Add rice and stir 2 minutes. Add wine and let it reduce.
Add hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often and adding more as it is absorbed.
Add saffron infusion halfway through. Cook rice 16-20 minutes until tender with a slightly firm center.
Turn off the heat and stir in remaining butter and Parmesan. Season and serve with a flowing consistency.
tips: Keep stock hot and serve the rice fluid rather than compact.

r-fr-coq-au-vin.summary: Chicken braised in red wine with bacon, mushrooms and pearl onions.
r-fr-coq-au-vin.history: Coq au vin belongs to the French tradition of braising poultry in wine. It is especially associated with Burgundy, with versions in other wine regions.
steps: Brown bacon in a pot and remove. Dry the chicken and brown in batches with the oil.
Add carrots, onions and garlic; cook 5 minutes. Sprinkle in flour and stir 1 minute.
Add wine and stock, scraping the bottom. Add chicken, bacon, thyme and bay leaf.
Cover and simmer gently 60 minutes. Add mushrooms and cook another 20 minutes until tender and the chicken reaches 74 °C.
Remove bay leaf and season. Reduce the sauce uncovered if necessary.
tips: Use a wine you would drink and simmer gently to keep the chicken juicy.

r-fr-bouillabaisse.summary: Fish stew with saffron, fennel and orange, served with toasted bread and rouille.
r-fr-bouillabaisse.history: A Marseille specialty linked to fishing communities. Species and serving styles vary; this home version uses accessible fish and prepared stock.
ingredients: 1.2 kg cleaned firm fish pieces, such as monkfish, sea bass and rockfish
1 strip orange peel without white pith
6 slices toasted bread and 100 g prepared rouille
steps: Sauté onion and fennel in oil for 10 minutes. Add garlic and tomatoes and cook another 10 minutes.
Add stock, saffron and orange peel. Simmer 15 minutes.
Add thicker fish pieces first, then smaller ones. Cook 8-12 minutes depending on thickness, until opaque and at 63 °C.
Remove the orange peel, season and serve fish and broth with rouille-spread toast.
tips: Add large fish pieces first and remove smaller ones when cooked.

r-es-paella-valenciana.summary: Valencian rice with chicken, rabbit, green beans, garrofó beans and saffron.
r-es-paella-valenciana.history: Paella valenciana is linked with Valencia’s rice-growing culture. This meat-and-vegetable combination represents one traditional preparation.
ingredients: 600 g chicken and 400 g rabbit, cut into pieces
1.5 liters hot water, adjusted to the rice
steps: Brown chicken and rabbit in oil in a wide paella pan for 15 minutes.
Add beans and tomato. Cook 5 minutes; add paprika, then immediately water and saffron.
Simmer 20 minutes. Adjust salt and spread the rice evenly.
Cook without stirring about 18 minutes, first at medium heat then low, following the rice’s liquid instructions. Check 74 °C in chicken and 71 °C in rabbit.
Add rosemary toward the end, turn off the heat and rest 5 minutes.
tips: Spread rice evenly and avoid stirring after adding the stock.

r-es-gazpacho.summary: Cold tomato, cucumber and pepper soup emulsified with olive oil and sherry vinegar.
r-es-gazpacho.history: Andalusian gazpacho comes from southern Spain. Ratios of vegetables, bread and vinegar vary between households.
ingredients: 100 ml cold water, adjusted as needed
steps: Soak the bread in some of the water for 5 minutes.
Wash and chop tomatoes, cucumber and pepper. Blend with garlic, bread and vinegar.
Drizzle in oil while blending to emulsify. Add salt and water to make a light soup.
Strain if desired and refrigerate at least 1 hour. Stir before serving.
tips: Taste salt and vinegar after chilling because the soup’s flavor changes slightly.

r-de-sauerbraten.summary: German beef roast marinated in wine and vinegar, slowly braised and served with a spiced sauce.
r-de-sauerbraten.history: Sauerbraten has regional German variations; the Rhineland version often balances sour and sweet. This recipe is associated with that region without claiming a particular inventor.
ingredients: 6 juniper berries, 3 cloves and 2 bay leaves
steps: Mix wine, vinegar, water, vegetables and spices. Submerge beef in a nonreactive container and marinate covered in the refrigerator for 3 days, turning daily.
Remove and dry the meat, reserving the marinade. Brown the meat on all sides in oil.
Add vegetables and marinade. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer 2.5-3 hours until very tender.
Remove the meat. Strain the sauce, add crumbled gingerbread and simmer while stirring until thickened.
Slice the beef and serve with the sauce, adjusting salt and pepper.
tips: Always marinate in the refrigerator in glass or stainless steel.

r-gr-moussaka.summary: Layers of eggplant and lamb with tomato, topped with béchamel and browned cheese.
r-gr-moussaka.history: Moussaka has many eastern Mediterranean variations. This baked béchamel version is associated with modern Greek cooking.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Brush eggplant with half the oil and bake 20-25 minutes, turning halfway.
Sauté onion in remaining oil. Add and break up lamb, then add tomato, cinnamon, salt and pepper; cook 20 minutes.
Melt butter, add flour and stir 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in milk until thickened, then add nutmeg and half the cheese.
Layer eggplant and meat in a baking dish. Cover with béchamel and remaining cheese.
Bake at 180 °C for 35-40 minutes until golden and at 74 °C in the center. Rest 15 minutes before slicing.
tips: Rest before cutting so the layers hold their shape.

r-pt-bacalhau.summary: Shredded cod with matchstick potatoes, onion and eggs, finished with olives and parsley.
r-pt-bacalhau.history: Bacalhau à Brás is a Portuguese preparation strongly associated with Lisbon. Its texture depends on combining potatoes and eggs just before serving.
ingredients: 1 sliced onion and 2 chopped garlic cloves
steps: If the cod is still salted, soak it in the refrigerator for 24-48 hours, changing the water; the listed times start with already desalted cod.
Remove skin and bones and shred the fish. Fry potatoes in batches until golden and drain.
Sauté onion and garlic in olive oil. Add cod and cook until opaque and at 63 °C.
Add potatoes and beaten eggs. Stir over low heat until the eggs set, leaving no liquid egg.
Add olives and parsley, taste before salting and serve immediately.
tips: Taste the fish before salting and count desalting separately if starting with dry salt cod.

r-it-tiramisu.summary: Layered coffee and mascarpone dessert with optional Marsala and pasteurized eggs.
r-it-tiramisu.history: Tiramisu is associated with Treviso and northeastern Italy. Its creation has competing claims; Marsala is an optional variation.
steps: Prepare and cool the coffee. Add Marsala if using.
Beat pasteurized yolks with sugar until thick and mix with mascarpone.
Beat pasteurized whites in a clean bowl and gently fold into the cream.
Briefly dip ladyfingers in coffee and alternate layers of biscuits and cream in a dish.
Cover and refrigerate at least 4 hours. Dust with cocoa just before serving and keep refrigerated.
tips: Pasteurized eggs are necessary for this uncooked preparation.

r-it-osso-buco.summary: Veal shanks gently braised with wine and vegetables, finished with lemon and parsley gremolata.
r-it-osso-buco.history: Ossobuco is a Lombard specialty associated with Milan, made with cross-cut shanks containing bone and marrow.
ingredients: 4 bone-in veal shank slices, about 1.2 kg
1 carrot, 1 celery stalk and 1 onion, chopped
1 garlic clove and 3 tablespoons parsley, chopped
steps: Dry and season the veal, dust lightly with flour and brown in oil. Remove.
Sauté onion, celery and carrot. Add wine and scrape the pan; reduce 2 minutes.
Add stock and tomato paste. Return meat, cover and braise very gently about 2 hours until tender.
Mix lemon zest, garlic and parsley to make the gremolata.
Serve meat with its sauce and scatter gremolata over the top just before serving.
tips: Avoid hard boiling; gentle cooking better preserves the shank and its marrow.

r-fr-ratatouille.summary: Provençal stew of eggplant, zucchini, peppers and tomatoes with olive oil and herbs.
r-fr-ratatouille.history: Ratatouille is associated with Nice and Provençal seasonal vegetables. This diced version cooks vegetables separately to retain texture.
steps: Cut eggplant, zucchini and peppers into similarly sized cubes.
Brown eggplant in some oil and remove. Repeat with zucchini and peppers to avoid overcooking.
Sauté onion and garlic in remaining oil; add tomatoes and herbs and cook 15 minutes.
Combine all vegetables and simmer 15-20 minutes until tender but still holding their shape.
Season and serve hot or warm.
tips: Brown vegetables in batches to concentrate flavor without turning them into purée.

r-fr-crêpes.summary: Thin crêpes in orange and butter sauce; liqueur is optional and no flambéing is needed.
r-fr-crêpes.history: Crêpes Suzette are a classic French dessert with different stories about their creation. This is a home adaptation without an open flame.
steps: Whisk flour, eggs, milk, salt and 20 g melted butter. Rest the batter 20 minutes.
Cook thin crêpes in a lightly greased nonstick pan, about 1 minute on the first side and a few seconds on the other.
Melt the remaining 60 g butter with sugar, juice and zest. Cook 5 minutes to make a light sauce.
Fold crêpes into quarters and warm in the sauce. If using liqueur, remove from heat to add it, then warm gently.
Serve immediately. This home version is prepared without flambéing.
tips: Keep the skillet off the heat when adding liqueur and do not ignite it.

r-es-tortilla.summary: Potato and onion omelet, golden outside and fully set in the center.
r-es-tortilla.history: Potato tortilla is made throughout Spain, with and without onion. Its origin is not assigned exclusively to Pamplona here.
ingredients: 200 ml olive oil for cooking potatoes
steps: Heat oil over medium-low heat. Cook potatoes and onion 20-25 minutes until tender without browning too much.
Drain and reserve the oil for other cooking. Beat eggs with salt and mix with the warm potatoes.
Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a 22 cm nonstick skillet. Add mixture and cook on low until the base is firm.
Turn using a plate covering the pan and slide back in. Cook until the center reaches 71 °C and no liquid egg remains.
Rest 5 minutes before cutting.
tips: Use a plate wider than the skillet and dry oven mitts to turn carefully.

r-es-pulpo-gallego.summary: Tender cooked octopus served with potatoes, paprika, olive oil and coarse salt.
r-es-pulpo-gallego.history: Associated with Galicia and its fairs, this dish is also called pulpo á feira. Potato is a frequent, though not universal, accompaniment.
ingredients: 1 cleaned octopus, 1.2 kg, thawed in the refrigerator
steps: Bring a large pot of water with bay leaf to a boil. Add octopus and simmer 40-60 minutes, depending on size, until a skewer enters easily.
Meanwhile, boil the whole potatoes separately for 25-35 minutes until tender.
Rest octopus in its water for 10 minutes, drain and slice the tentacles.
Peel and slice potatoes. Arrange octopus on top and finish with paprika, coarse salt and oil.
tips: Timing depends on size; check tenderness with a skewer before removing.

r-de-schnitzel.summary: Thin breaded veal cutlets fried with a light, crisp coating.
r-de-schnitzel.history: Wiener Schnitzel is associated with Vienna and Austrian cooking. Although served in Germany too, this recipe is registered in Austria.
steps: Pound veal between sheets of cooking paper to about 4 mm thick. Season lightly.
Coat each cutlet in flour, egg and breadcrumbs without pressing the coating too firmly.
Heat clarified butter in a wide skillet. Fry in batches 2-3 minutes per side until golden and at 63 °C in the center.
Drain on a rack and rest 3 minutes. Serve with lemon.
tips: Do not press breadcrumbs firmly against the meat, keeping the coating lighter.

r-de-spaetzle.summary: Fresh egg noodles combined with melted cheese and browned onions.
r-de-spaetzle.history: Käsespätzle is prepared in Swabia and other Alpine areas. This version is linked to Baden-Württemberg and centers on the noodles.
ingredients: 150 g Emmental and 100 g Gruyère, grated
1 teaspoon salt and pepper to taste
steps: Mix flour, eggs, salt and water into a thick batter that falls slowly from a spoon. Rest 10 minutes.
Slowly brown onions in butter, stirring, about 20 minutes.
Press batter through a spätzle maker into boiling salted water. Cook in batches until floating, then 1 minute longer; lift out.
Layer hot noodles and cheese in a dish. Bake at 200 °C about 10 minutes until melted.
Top with browned onion, season with pepper and serve.
tips: The thick batter must pass through the utensil; add water a spoonful at a time.

r-gr-souvlaki.summary: Greek chicken skewers marinated with lemon, garlic and oregano, served in pita with tzatziki.
r-gr-souvlaki.history: Souvlaki refers to Greek skewered meat preparations. This chicken version uses common accompaniments without claiming exclusive Athenian origins.
ingredients: 600 g boneless chicken, in 3 cm cubes
1 teaspoon oregano and 2 chopped garlic cloves
steps: Mix oil, lemon, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper. Add chicken and marinate covered in the refrigerator for 1 hour.
Thread onto skewers; soak wooden skewers beforehand according to their maker’s instructions.
Grill over medium-high heat for 10-15 minutes, turning to brown all sides, until the center reaches 74 °C.
Warm pitas and serve with chicken, tzatziki, tomatoes and onion.
tips: Cut chicken in even cubes so all skewers cook at the same rate.

r-pt-pasteis.summary: Portuguese puff-pastry tartlets filled with egg-yolk custard and browned on top.
r-pt-pasteis.history: Pastéis de nata are part of Portuguese baking and historically associated with Lisbon and Belém. This is a home version, not a bakery’s commercial formula.
steps: Heat oven to 240 °C. Roll pastry into a cylinder, cut 12 portions and press into tart molds.
Mix flour with some cold milk. Heat the remaining milk with cream and sugar; whisk in the flour mixture and cook until thickened.
Remove from heat. Temper yolks with a few spoonfuls of hot cream, combine and add vanilla.
Strain and fill molds three-quarters full. Bake 15-20 minutes until pastry is cooked and custard has browned spots.
Let cool slightly before unmolding and serve with cinnamon.
tips: Do not fill molds to the rim because the custard rises during baking.
